title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Australia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Australia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide across Australia: Medical Certificate of Cause of Death or Coroner clearance, appointing a funeral director (AFDA) and State/Territory Births, Deaths and Marriages (BDM) registration, Services Australia (Centrelink/Medicare) and Australian Death Notification Service, superannuation death benefits, and Supreme Court probate & ATO final tax return.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In Australia, medical certification, civil death registration, funeral regulation, and probate are governed by the state or territory where the death occurred, while social security, Medicare, passports, superannuation rules, and taxation are administered at the federal level. Below are the five main official and practical steps to follow in order.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death
steps.html:
Before a funeral director can transfer the deceased or arrange burial or cremation, a medical practitioner must verify the death and issue the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD), or the state or territory Coroner must issue clearance [3][4][5]:

  • Death in a hospital, hospice, or residential aged care facility: The attending doctor or authorised medical officer verifies the death, completes the MCCD, and coordinates with facility staff to care for the body until your appointed funeral director arrives [3][4].
  • Expected death at home under palliative care: Contact the treating general practitioner (GP) or community palliative care team according to the care plan (you do not need to call emergency services for an expected natural death at home if a doctor can attend and certify the cause of death) [3][4]. Once the doctor signs the MCCD, your chosen funeral director can transfer the deceased into their care [3].
  • Unexpected, sudden, or unexplained death (at home or in a public place): Call Triple Zero (000) immediately for police and ambulance attendance, and do not move the body or disturb the surroundings [3][4][5]. Where a doctor cannot certify a natural cause of death, or where the death was sudden, accidental, or reportable under state law, police refer the matter to the State or Territory Coroner (such as the Coroners Court of Victoria, the NSW State Coroner, or the Coroners Court of Queensland), who investigates the cause of death and issues the release and burial or cremation authorisation [3][4][5].

steps.title: Appoint a Funeral Director and Register the Death with State or Territory BDM
steps.html:
Check whether your family member held a pre-paid funeral contract, funeral bond, or funeral insurance policy, and appoint a funeral director to coordinate the funeral and official registration [1][6]:

  • Locating a funeral provider: You can search for member funeral directors across all states and territories through the Australian Funeral Directors Association (now operating as Funerals Australia) at 03 9859 9966 or info@afda.org.au [6].
  • State or Territory Births, Deaths and Marriages (BDM) registration: In Australia, the appointed funeral director normally submits the official death registration statement (together with the doctor's MCCD or Coroner's certificate) directly to the relevant state or territory registry - typically within 7 days in New South Wales or 14 days in Victoria and Queensland [3][4][5]. The funeral director also orders the official Death Certificate on behalf of the next of kin or executor from the relevant registry, such as the NSW Registry of Births, Deaths & Marriages (13 77 88) [3], Births, Deaths and Marriages Victoria (1300 369 367) [4], or the Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages (13 74 68) [5].

steps.title: Notify Services Australia, Government Agencies, and Financial Institutions
steps.html:
Promptly notifying government bodies stops ongoing benefit payments (preventing overpayments that the estate must repay) and updates official identity records [1]:

  • Services Australia (Centrelink, Medicare, and Child Support): Notify Services Australia within 28 days by calling the Centrelink bereavement line on 132 300 (or Medicare on 132 011), visiting a service centre, or submitting an Advice of Death form [1]. A single notification to Services Australia updates both Centrelink and Medicare records [1].
  • My Aged Care and state agencies: If the deceased received government-subsidised home care or residential aged care, notify My Aged Care on 1800 200 422 [1]. Cancel their Australian passport through the Australian Passport Office (131 232), and cancel their driver licence, vehicle registration, and electoral roll entry through your state or territory service agency (such as Service NSW, VicRoads, or Transport and Main Roads in Queensland) [1][3].
  • Australian Death Notification Service (ADNS): Once you receive the official BDM Death Certificate, you can use the free, government-backed Australian Death Notification Service (operated jointly by the state and territory BDM registries) to notify multiple participating banks, superannuation funds, insurers, utilities, and telecommunications companies in a single online submission [7].

steps.title: Check Bereavement Payments and Claim Superannuation Death Benefits
steps.html:
• Services Australia bereavement assistance: Depending on family relationship and benefit status, a surviving partner (spouse or de facto partner) or carer who was receiving a qualifying pension, income support payment, or Carer Payment from Services Australia may be eligible for a lump-sum bereavement payment or a 14-week continuation period to assist with the transition [1][2]. Check eligibility when you call Services Australia on 132 300 [1][2].
  • Superannuation death benefits and life insurance inside super: In Australia, a person's superannuation balance (and any life insurance held inside the super fund) does not automatically form part of their estate governed by their will [9]. Contact the deceased's superannuation fund trustee immediately (if you do not know which fund they used, the executor can trace lost or held superannuation through the Australian Taxation Office on 13 28 61) [8][9]. If the deceased left a valid Binding Death Benefit Nomination, the trustee must pay the death benefit to the nominated dependants (such as a spouse, child, or person in an interdependency relationship) or to the Legal Personal Representative (the estate executor or administrator); otherwise, the trustee distributes the benefit under fund rules [9]. Under federal tax law, lump-sum superannuation death benefits paid to a tax-law dependant (such as a spouse or child under 18) are tax-free, whereas taxable components paid to adult non-dependent children are subject to superannuation death benefits tax [9].

steps.title: Administer the Estate, Apply for Supreme Court Probate, and Lodge Final ATO Tax Returns
steps.html:
The executor named in the will (or the next of kin if there is no valid will) acts as the Legal Personal Representative (LPR) to settle the estate [3][8]:

  • Locating the will and applying for Probate or Letters of Administration: Locate the original will and check with the deceased's banks, share registries, and the state land titles office whether a formal court grant is required before assets can be released or transferred (small bank balances are often released with a certified Death Certificate, will, and indemnity form, whereas real estate held solely in the deceased's name or larger financial accounts require a court grant) [3][5]. Where required, the executor applies to the Probate Office of the relevant State or Territory Supreme Court (for example, the Supreme Court of NSW, the Supreme Court of Victoria, or the Supreme Court of Queensland) for a Grant of Probate (or, if there is no valid will, the next of kin applies for Letters of Administration) [3][5].
  • Notifying the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) and lodging final tax returns: The Legal Personal Representative must submit an official notification of death to the Australian Taxation Office (13 28 61) with a certified copy of the Death Certificate and the will or grant of probate/administration [8]. If the deceased met tax lodgement criteria, the LPR must lodge a final individual Date of Death tax return covering the period from 1 July up to the date of death (and, if the estate earns taxable income or capital gains after the date of death, a separate Deceased Estate Trust tax return) before making final distributions to beneficiaries [8].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in United States: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In the United States, death registration, burial and cremation permits, and estate probate are governed primarily by state and county law, while survivor benefits and final income tax filings are handled at the federal level [1][2]. Below is a 5-step guide to the official process.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and Official Certification of Death
steps.html:
Before a funeral home can complete civil registration or arrange burial or cremation, an authorized medical professional or medico-legal authority must pronounce the death and complete the medical portion of the death certificate [1][2].

  • Death in a hospital, nursing home, or under hospice care: When a person dies in a hospital or licensed care facility, the attending physician, nurse practitioner, or medical staff pronounces the death, completes the medical cause-of-death certification (typically through the state's Electronic Death Registration System), and coordinates release of the body to the family's appointed funeral home [1][2]. If your family member died at home under registered hospice care, call the hospice nurse on duty rather than emergency services so the hospice team can pronounce the death and arrange release without an unnecessary emergency investigation [1].
  • Unexpected or unattended death at home or in a public place: If the death occurs suddenly at home without hospice supervision or in a public place, call 911 immediately [1]. Local law enforcement and emergency medical services will respond and notify the county Coroner or Medical Examiner (for example, the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in New York City or the County Department of Medical Examiner in Los Angeles County) [1][2]. For sudden, accidental, unexplained, or unattended deaths, the Coroner or Medical Examiner takes legal jurisdiction to determine the cause and manner of death, conduct an examination or autopsy if required by state statute, and issue the official medical certification and release before the funeral director can transfer your family member [1][2].

steps.title: Check Pre-Arrangements and Appoint a Licensed Funeral Provider
steps.html:
Before signing a funeral contract, check your family member's records for a pre-need funeral contract, burial insurance, life insurance policy, or eligibility for veterans burial benefits [1][3].

  • Appointing a licensed funeral home: In almost all U.S. states, a state-licensed funeral director coordinates the physical care and transport of the deceased, files the death certificate with the local registrar, and obtains the burial-transit or cremation permit [2][4]. You can locate a state-licensed provider through the directory of the National Funeral Directors Association (phone: +1 262-789-1880; email: nfda@nfda.org) [4]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual providers.
  • Consumer protections under the FTC Funeral Rule: Under the federal Funeral Rule enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (phone: +1 877-382-4357), every funeral provider must give you an itemized General Price List (GPL) in writing when you begin discussing arrangements and provide price information over the phone upon request [3]. You have the legal right to purchase only the specific goods and services you select, to use a casket or urn purchased from a third-party vendor without paying a handling fee, and to decline embalming unless your specific state law requires it after a set time or for specialized transport (refrigeration is an accepted alternative in most jurisdictions) [3].
  • Statutory burial and cremation timelines: Timelines and waiting periods are set by state law. Many states require cremation or burial permits to be issued only after a mandatory waiting period (commonly 24 to 48 hours after death, as in Texas or New York) and require specific authorization from the Coroner or Medical Examiner before cremation can proceed [2][4].

steps.title: Register the Death with State or County Vital Records and Obtain Death Certificates
steps.html:
Your appointed funeral director normally gathers your family member's personal and demographic information (including full legal name, Social Security number, date and place of birth, parents' names, and occupation) and files the official death record with the local county health department or state Office of Vital Statistics / Vital Records within the statutory state deadline (typically 3 to 5 days after death, depending on the state) [1][2].

  • Burial-transit permits and certified Death Certificates: Once the death is registered, the local registrar issues the official burial, cremation, or transit permit required before final disposition [2]. Order 5 to 10 certified copies of the official Death Certificate through the funeral home at the time of registration or directly from the state or county Vital Records office (retrievable through the directory on USA.gov at +1 844-872-4681), as banks, life insurers, pension administrators, and probate courts require certified copies bearing an official raised or multicolored seal [1][2].
  • If a U.S. citizen dies abroad: When a U.S. citizen dies outside the United States, the death is registered first with the local foreign civil registry, and the U.S. Department of State (Overseas Citizens Services phone: +1 888-407-4747 from the U.S./Canada or +1 202-501-4444 from abroad) through the nearest U.S. Embassy or Consulate issues the Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad (CRDA, Form DS-2060), which serves as official English-language proof of death across all U.S. states [5].

steps.title: Claim Social Security, Veterans, and Survivor Benefits
steps.html:
Promptly notify federal benefit agencies to prevent overpayments (any monthly benefit paid for the month of death or later must be returned) and to apply for survivor entitlements [1][6]:

  • Social Security Administration (SSA): Although the funeral director can report the death to Social Security if you supply your family member's Social Security number, you must contact the Social Security Administration directly by calling 1-800-772-1213 (TTY: 1-800-325-0778; or through the relevant U.S. Embassy Federal Benefits Unit if residing abroad) to claim benefits, as survivor claims cannot be completed online [6]. Depending on your relationship to the deceased and their work credits, eligible family members (such as a surviving spouse, eligible divorced spouse, minor or disabled child, or dependent parent) may qualify for monthly Social Security survivor benefits and a one-time lump-sum death payment of $255 [6].
  • U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA): If your family member served in the U.S. Armed Forces, contact the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (phone: +1 800-827-1000; National Cemetery Scheduling Office: +1 800-535-1117) to check eligibility for burial in a VA national cemetery at no cost, a government headstone or marker, a burial flag, a Presidential Memorial Certificate, VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) or Survivors Pension, and monetary burial allowances claimed via VA Form 21P-530EZ [7].
  • Employer benefits and life insurance: Contact your family member's current or former employers, labor unions, and pension plan administrators regarding unpaid wages, 401(k) or IRA retirement accounts, and employer-sponsored group life insurance [1].

steps.title: Complete Probate / Estate Administration, Notify Banks, and File Final Tax Returns
steps.html:
The legal process for settling your family member's assets and liabilities depends on how assets were titled and the laws of the state where your family member was domiciled [1]:

  • State Probate Court and estate succession: Locate the original will or trust documents [1]. File the will with the county Probate Court (also called the Surrogate's Court in states like New York and New Jersey, or Orphans' Court in Pennsylvania and Maryland) in the county where the deceased resided [1]. If probate is required, the court appoints the executor (Letters Testamentary) or, if there is no will, an administrator (Letters of Administration). Most states offer a simplified Small Estate Affidavit procedure when probate assets fall below a state-specific statutory threshold (for example, in California, Texas, or Illinois), while assets with designated beneficiaries (life insurance, retirement accounts, payable-on-death bank accounts, and joint tenancy property) generally transfer outside probate upon presentation of a certified Death Certificate [1].
  • Notifying banks, creditors, and credit bureaus: Present certified copies of the Death Certificate and court-issued Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration to banks and financial institutions to close or retitled sole accounts and open an estate bank account if needed [1]. Notify the three major credit reporting bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) to place a deceased alert on the credit file and prevent identity theft [1].
  • Federal and state tax filings (IRS): The court-appointed personal representative or surviving person responsible for the estate must file the deceased's final federal income tax return on Form 1040 or Form 1040-SR with the Internal Revenue Service (phone: +1 800-829-1040) by the standard April 15 deadline of the year following death [8]. Write the word Deceased, your family member's name, and the date of death across the top of Form 1040 [8]. If the estate earns gross income of $600 or more after the date of death, you must also obtain an estate Employer Identification Number (EIN) and file a fiduciary income tax return (IRS Form 1041), alongside any applicable state income or inheritance tax returns [8].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in United Kingdom: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in United Kingdom: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in United Kingdom: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In the United Kingdom, the exact procedures and statutory registration deadlines depend on whether the death occurred in England and Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland [1][2]. Below is a 5-step guide covering the official UK framework.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death
steps.html:
Before a death can be registered, an authorized medical practitioner must verify the death and issue the official medical certificate, or the case must be cleared by the coroner or procurator fiscal [1][2].

  • Expected death in a hospital, care home, or at home: In England and Wales, an attending doctor completes the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD), which is then independently scrutinized and countersigned by an NHS Medical Examiner [1][2]. The Medical Examiner's office contacts the next of kin or informant to explain the recorded cause of death, answer questions about care, and confirm when the MCCD has been sent electronically to the local Register Office [2]. In Scotland, the attending doctor issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Form 11), and in Northern Ireland, the doctor issues the MCCD for registration [1][3]. If an expected death occurs at home, call the person's GP or NHS 111 so a clinician can verify the death [1][2].
  • Sudden, unexpected, or unexplained death outside a hospital: If the death is sudden, accidental, unexplained, or occurs in a public place, call 999 immediately so emergency services and the police can attend [1][2]. When a doctor cannot certify a natural cause of death, the death is referred to the local Coroner (in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) or to the Procurator Fiscal via the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (in Scotland) [1][2][3]. Civil registration waits until the Coroner or Procurator Fiscal issues formal release paperwork or an interim certificate of the fact of death after any necessary post-mortem inquiry [2][3].

steps.title: Check Funeral Pre-Arrangements and Appoint a Funeral Director
steps.html:
Before making financial commitments, check your family member's paperwork for a prepaid funeral plan, over-50s life insurance policy, or written funeral wishes [1][3].

  • Appointing an accredited funeral provider: You can contact a funeral director as soon as you are ready to arrange the transfer and care of your family member, even before civil registration is finalized (though the burial or cremation itself cannot proceed until registration or coronial clearance is complete) [1][2]. To find a provider adhering to inspected professional standards and transparent itemized pricing, you can search the directories of the National Association of Funeral Directors (phone: +44 121 711 1343; email: info@nafd.org.uk) or the National Society of Allied and Independent Funeral Directors (phone: +44 1279 726777; email: info@saif.org.uk) [4][5]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual funeral providers.
  • Statutory burial and cremation requirements: Your funeral director coordinates the booking of the cemetery or crematorium and receives the registrar's Certificate for Burial or Cremation (the Green Form in England and Wales, or Form 14 in Scotland) or the Coroner's Order for Burial / Cremation Form 6 before the funeral takes place [1][2][3].

steps.title: Register the Death at the Local Register Office and Use Tell Us Once
steps.html:
Once the Medical Examiner's office (or doctor/coroner) confirms that the medical certificate has been sent to the registrar, book an appointment at the local Register Office via GOV.UK (or mygov.scot in Scotland / nidirect in Northern Ireland) [1][2][3].

  • Statutory registration deadlines: You must register the death within 5 days in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (which begins from when the Register Office receives the MCCD from the Medical Examiner in England and Wales), or within 8 days in Scotland [1][2][3]. Provide the deceased's full name, date and place of birth, last address, occupation, NHS number, National Insurance number, and details of any spouse or civil partner [2].
  • Certificates issued at registration: The registrar issues the Certificate for Burial or Cremation free of charge for your funeral director, and you should purchase several certified copies of the official Death Certificate (at the statutory fee, currently £12.50 per copy in England and Wales) for banks, insurers, and probate [1][2].
  • Notifying government departments via Tell Us Once: During your registration appointment in England, Wales, or Scotland, ask the registrar for a unique reference number for the GOV.UK Tell Us Once service [1][2]. Tell Us Once notifies HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC), the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), the Passport Office, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), local councils, and public sector pension schemes in a single step [1][2]. (If a British national dies outside the UK, you should follow the consular bereavement guidance of the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and register the death locally in the country of death [1]).

steps.title: Claim Statutory Funeral Grants, Survivor Pensions, and Bereavement Benefits
steps.html:
Depending on your relationship to the deceased and your household circumstances, contact the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP Bereavement Service phone: 0800 151 2012; or the International Pension Centre at +44 191 218 7777 if living abroad) to check benefit entitlements [1][6]:

  • Bereavement Support Payment: A surviving spouse, civil partner, or cohabiting partner (where there are dependent children or pregnancy at the time of bereavement) whose deceased partner paid qualifying National Insurance contributions (or died due to a work-related cause) while the survivor was under State Pension age may qualify for Bereavement Support Payment, which consists of an initial lump sum (£3,500 higher rate with children, or £2,500 standard rate) and up to 18 monthly payments (£350 or £100) [6]. Apply within 3 months of the death to receive the full 18 monthly payments (claims can be made up to 21 months after death for a reduced number of payments) [6].
  • Funeral Expenses Payment (or Funeral Support Payment in Scotland): If you receive qualifying means-tested benefits such as Universal Credit or Pension Credit and are arranging the funeral, you can apply to the Department for Work and Pensions (on Form SF200 within 6 months of the funeral) or Social Security Scotland for help toward burial or cremation fees and funeral costs [1][3].

steps.title: Notify Banks, HM Revenue & Customs, and Apply for Probate or Confirmation
steps.html:
To settle your family member's financial affairs, property, and tax obligations [1][7]:

  • Notifying banks, insurers, and pension providers: Provide certified Death Certificates to banks, building societies, mortgage lenders, life insurers, and private pension schemes [1]. Many UK financial institutions participate in the Death Notification Service, allowing you to notify multiple banks simultaneously, and banks may release small balances or pay the funeral director's invoice directly from the deceased's account before probate is granted [1].
  • Tax and Inheritance Tax (HMRC): If you did not use Tell Us Once, notify HM Revenue & Customs (Bereavement Helpline: 0300 200 3300; Inheritance Tax Helpline: 0300 123 1072) to finalize the person's Income Tax up to the date of death and check whether the estate owes Inheritance Tax (IHT, generally due within 6 months from the end of the month of death, using form IHT400 where required) [1][7].
  • Applying for Grant of Probate (or Confirmation in Scotland): Locate the original will [1][7]. If the estate includes sole property or financial assets above the banks' small-estate thresholds, the executor named in the will applies to HM Courts & Tribunals Service via GOV.UK for a Grant of Probate in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (or the nearest entitled relative applies for Letters of Administration if there is no will) [7]. In Scotland, the executor applies to the local Sheriff Court Commissariot for Confirmation [3][7].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ireland: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Ireland: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in Ireland: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In Ireland, every death must be medically certified or referred to the Coroner before being registered with the Civil Registration Service, and funeral arrangements can proceed once medical certification or coronial release is issued via Citizens Information [1][2]. Below is a 5-step guide to the official Irish procedures.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and the Death Notification Form (DNF)
steps.html:
How a death is medically certified in Ireland depends on where the death occurred and whether a registered medical practitioner attended the deceased recently [1][2]:

  • Expected death in a hospital, nursing home, or at home: When a person dies of natural causes in a hospital, hospice, or care facility, or at home under the care of a general practitioner (GP) who saw or treated the patient within the 28 days before death, the attending doctor verifies the death and completes Part 1 of the official Death Notification Form (DNF), which contains the Medical Certificate of the Cause of Death [1][2][3]. If an expected death occurs at home, contact the person's GP or out-of-hours GP service so the doctor can attend and issue the DNF [1].
  • Sudden, unexpected, or unnatural death outside a hospital: If the death is sudden, unexplained, accidental, or occurs in a public place, or if no doctor attended the deceased within 28 days prior to death, call 999 or 112 immediately [1][2]. An Garda Síochána and emergency medical services will attend and report the death to the local Coroner (for example, the Dublin District Coroner or the relevant county Coroner) [1][2]. In Coroner cases, a doctor does not issue a Death Notification Form; instead, the Coroner authorizes transfer to a mortuary, directs a post-mortem examination or inquest if required, releases the body for burial or cremation, and registers the death directly once inquiries conclude [1][2]. While coronial inquiries are ongoing, you can request an Interim Certificate of the Fact of Death from the Coroner to notify banks, the Department of Social Protection, and the Revenue Commissioners [1][2].

steps.title: Check Pre-Arrangements and Appoint a Funeral Director
steps.html:
Before making financial commitments, check your family member's records for a prepaid funeral plan, credit union death benefit or insurance policy, or life assurance policy [1].

  • Appointing a funeral director: In Ireland, you can appoint a funeral director as soon as a doctor has confirmed the death (or once the Coroner authorizes release of the remains); you do not need to wait until the civil registration is completed to hold the funeral [1][2]. You can locate a professional funeral provider bound by an industry code of practice through the directory of the Irish Association of Funeral Directors (phone: +353 818 935 000; email: info@iafd.ie) [4]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual funeral providers.
  • Burial and cremation paperwork: Your funeral director coordinates the care of the deceased, burial plot opening or cemetery paperwork, or cremation medical referee forms (when cremation is chosen, a separate medical cremation form signed by the attending doctor and reviewed by an independent medical referee, or a Coroner's Cremation Certificate, is required before cremation can take place) [1][4].

steps.title: Register the Death with the HSE Civil Registration Service
steps.html:
Under the Civil Registration Act 2004, every death occurring in the State must be registered with the HSE Civil Registration Service / General Register Office (GRO phone: +353 90 663 2900) [2][3][5]:

  • Statutory 3-month deadline and how to register: For non-coronial deaths, a qualified informant (usually a close family member) must register the death within 3 months of the date of death [1][2]. Complete Part 2 of the Death Notification Form (DNF) with the deceased's Personal Public Service (PPS) number, date and place of birth, occupation, marital/civil status, and parents' names [2][3][5]. You can register the death in person at any HSE Civil Registration Service office nationwide (bringing the signed DNF and your own photo ID) or online via MyGovID where the doctor has submitted the medical certificate electronically [3][5].
  • Obtaining official Death Certificates: Registering the death is free of charge [2]. Order several full standard Death Certificates (€20 per copy, plus postage if ordered online via certificates.ie) for banks, insurers, and probate; a reduced-fee copy is issued for official social welfare use upon presenting a letter from the Department of Social Protection [1][2][5]. (If an Irish citizen dies abroad, the death is registered with the local foreign civil registry, and the Department of Foreign Affairs at +353 1 408 2000 or the nearest Irish Embassy provides consular assistance [1]).

steps.title: Notify the Department of Social Protection and Claim Survivor Pensions or Funeral Support
steps.html:
Notify the Department of Social Protection (DSP Bereavement and Pensions Helpline: 0818 200 400 or +353 1 471 5898; Sligo Pension Services Office: 0818 200 400) as soon as possible, quoting your family member's PPS number [1][6][7]:

  • Continuing payments and survivor pensions: Note that Ireland's contributory Bereavement Grant was discontinued in 2014 [1][6]. However, if the deceased was receiving a social welfare payment and had a qualified adult dependant (such as a spouse, civil partner, or cohabitant), that social welfare payment often continues for 6 weeks after the death [6]. Depending on your relationship to the deceased, a surviving spouse, civil partner, or eligible cohabitant may qualify for the Widowed or Surviving Civil Partner's (Contributory or Non-Contributory) Pension / Bereaved Partner's Pension, as well as the once-off Widowed or Surviving Civil Partner Grant (€8,000 where there is a dependent child) [6][7].
  • Additional funeral cost assistance (Additional Needs Payment): If you have low income or face financial hardship meeting funeral expenses, you can apply to the Department of Social Protection Community Welfare Service for a means-tested Additional Needs Payment under the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme [1][6].

steps.title: Notify Banks, the Revenue Commissioners, and Complete High Court Probate
steps.html:
To administer your family member's estate, bank accounts, and tax affairs [1][8]:

  • Notifying banks, credit unions, and insurers: Present an original Death Certificate to all banks, An Post (for State Savings), credit unions, life insurers, and private pension schemes [1]. Joint accounts held with right of survivorship typically transfer to the surviving joint holder upon presentation of the Death Certificate (subject to any Revenue clearance requirements for large balances), and credit unions pay funds nominated under a statutory Credit Union Nomination (up to the statutory cap) directly to the nominee without probate [1].
  • Tax clearance and filing with the Revenue Commissioners: Notify the Revenue Commissioners (National PAYE Helpline: +353 1 738 3636 or online via MyAccount / MyEnquiries) to finalize your family member's income tax up to the date of death [1][8]. Before applying for probate, the executor or administrator must submit the online Statement of Affairs (Probate) Form SA.2 through Revenue's myAccount or ROS portal [8]. Once submitted, Revenue issues the Notice of Acknowledgment (Probate), which is required by the Probate Office, and beneficiaries may have Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) reporting obligations depending on their relationship group threshold [8].
  • Applying for a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration: Locate the original will [1]. If the estate holds sole real property or sole bank balances above the financial institution's small-estate release threshold (commonly around €25,000, depending on the bank), the executor named in the will (or the next of kin if there is no will) must apply to the High Court Probate Office or District Probate Registry (part of the Courts Service of Ireland) for a Grant of Probate or Grant of Letters of Administration, either through a solicitor or via the Probate Office Personal Applicants process [1][8].

closingQuestion: To help us provide the exact local HSE Civil Registration office details and probate requirements, in which county in Ireland did the death occur, and did your family member leave a will?

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in New Zealand: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in New Zealand: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in New Zealand: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In New Zealand, medical certification or coronial clearance must take place before a burial or cremation can proceed, and the death must then be registered with Births, Deaths and Marriages within 3 working days after the funeral or cremation [1][2]. Below is a 5-step guide to the official process in New Zealand.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (HP4720)
steps.html:
Before your family member's body can be buried or cremated, a doctor or nurse practitioner must certify the cause of death, or the death must be cleared by the Coroner [1][2]:

  • Expected death in a hospital, hospice, rest home, or at home: When a person dies in a hospital, hospice, or aged-care facility, the medical staff on duty arrange for a doctor or nurse practitioner to examine the body and complete the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Form HP4720) via the Ministry of Health Death Documents system [1][2]. If an expected death occurs at home, call the person's general practitioner (GP) or palliative/hospice care team [2][3]. In New Zealand, there is no legal requirement to move the body immediately after a natural death, so family and whānau may take time before a funeral director transfers the deceased [2][3].
  • Sudden, unexpected, or accidental death outside a hospital: If the death is sudden, unexplained, accidental, or occurs in a public place, or if a doctor cannot determine the cause of death, call 111 immediately [2][3]. New Zealand Police will attend and report the death to the Duty Coroner through the National Initial Investigation Office (NIIO, phone: 0800 266 800) of Coronial Services of New Zealand [1][2]. When a death is referred to the Coroner, a standard HP4720 certificate is not issued; instead, the Coroner authorizes transfer to a mortuary, determines whether a post-mortem examination or inquiry is needed, and issues the Coroner's Authorization for Release of the Body so funeral arrangements can proceed [1][2].

steps.title: Check Pre-Arrangements and Appoint a Funeral Director
steps.html:
Before entering into a funeral contract, check your family member's paperwork for a prepaid funeral plan or trust, funeral insurance policy, or written wishes regarding burial, cremation, or tangihanga [2][3].

  • Appointing a funeral director: While New Zealand law permits families to manage a burial or cremation directly if they meet all local council cemetery and health regulations, most families appoint a professional funeral director to care for the deceased, obtain cremation medical referee approval (Form AB and Cremation Permission Form B where cremation is chosen), and file the death registration [1][4]. You can locate an accredited provider adhering to an industry code of ethics and transparent cost estimates through the Funeral Directors Association of New Zealand (phone: +64 4 473 7475; email: info@funeraldirectors.co.nz) [4]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual funeral providers.
  • Statutory burial and cremation requirements: A burial or cremation cannot take place until either the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (HP4720) or the Coroner's authorization has been issued, and for cremations, a Medical Referee has signed the permission to cremate [1][2].

steps.title: Register the Death with Births, Deaths and Marriages (DIA) Within 3 Working Days
steps.html:
Under the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act, every death in New Zealand must be registered with Births, Deaths and Marriages (BDM, part of the Department of Internal Affairs, phone: 0800 22 52 52 from New Zealand or +64 9 339 0852 from overseas) [1]:

  • Statutory 3-working-day deadline: The death must be registered within 3 working days after the burial or cremation of the body [1]. If you appoint a funeral director, they normally collect the demographic details from the family and submit the Death Registration (Form BDM 28) online to Births, Deaths and Marriages on your behalf [1]. If the family is managing the burial or cremation without a funeral director, the person in charge of the disposal must file the registration directly within 3 working days [1].
  • Official Death Certificates and Te Hokinga ā-Wairua: Order an official New Zealand Death Certificate through your funeral director or directly from Births, Deaths and Marriages, as banks, insurers, KiwiSaver providers, and the High Court require it for estate administration [1][2]. When registering the death, you can also use the government's Te Hokinga ā-Wairua End of Life Service on New Zealand Government (govt.nz) to coordinate notifications across public agencies (If a New Zealand citizen dies overseas, the death is registered locally abroad and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade SafeTravel consular team at +64 4 439 8000 can assist the family) [2][3].

steps.title: Claim Statutory Funeral Grants, Work and Income Support, and ACC Benefits
steps.html:
Depending on your household income, assets, and the cause of death, two main government bodies provide funeral grants and survivor entitlements [5][6]:

  • Work and Income (Ministry of Social Development - MSD): Contact Work and Income (general phone: 0800 559 009; NZ Superannuation / Senior Services phone: 0800 552 002) to report the death if your family member received New Zealand Superannuation, a Veteran's Pension, or a main benefit [5][6]. If the deceased's estate and surviving partner have limited income and assets, you can apply to Work and Income for a means-tested Funeral Grant to help toward necessary funeral costs, and surviving partners or caregivers of dependent children may qualify for continuation payments or survivor assistance [5][6].
  • Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) accidental death benefits: If your family member died as the result of an accident or injury covered by ACC, contact ACC (phone: 0800 101 996) to claim the statutory ACC Funeral Grant (which is not means-tested), the one-off Survivor's Grant for an eligible partner, child, or other dependant, and weekly compensation for surviving dependants [2][5].

steps.title: Notify Banks, KiwiSaver, Inland Revenue (IRD), and Apply for High Court Probate
steps.html:
To administer your family member's financial affairs, tax obligations, and estate [6][7]:

  • Small estates vs. High Court Probate or Letters of Administration: Locate the original will [3][6]. Under Section 65 of the Administration Act 1969, if the deceased held sole assets (such as a bank account, KiwiSaver account, or shares) exceeding $15,000 in any single institution, or owned real property in their sole name, the financial institution or Land Information New Zealand will require High Court authority before releasing or transferring the asset [6]. If there is a valid will, the named executor applies to the High Court Probate Registry (centralized in Wellington, Ministry of Justice phone: 0800 268 787) for a Grant of Probate; if there is no will, the entitled next of kin applies for Letters of Administration [6].
  • Notifying banks, KiwiSaver, and insurers: Provide certified copies of the Death Certificate (and Probate or Letters of Administration where required, or a small-estate statutory declaration for balances of $15,000 or less) to banks, life insurers, and the deceased's KiwiSaver scheme provider (as KiwiSaver balances do not pass by survivorship and are paid to the estate or personal representative) [6].
  • Notifying Inland Revenue (IRD): Notify Inland Revenue (phone: 0800 227 774 from New Zealand or +64 4 978 0779 from overseas, or via myIR) of the date of death and the details of the executor or administrator [7]. Inland Revenue will update the person's tax account, stop any Working for Families or child support payments, finalize individual income tax up to the date of death (including small tax refunds claimed via Form IR625 where there is no probate), and issue a new IRD number if a continuing estate tax return (Form IR6) is required [7].

closingQuestion: To help us tailor the next steps for you, did the death occur in a hospital or at home in New Zealand, and does the estate include sole assets over $15,000 or property requiring High Court Probate?

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in South Africa: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in South Africa: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in South Africa: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. In South Africa, every death must be medically certified on Form DHA-1663 (formerly BI-1663) and registered with the Department of Home Affairs to obtain a Burial Order before burial or cremation, and the estate must be reported to the Master of the High Court within 14 days [1][2]. Below is a 5-step guide to the official process in South Africa.

steps.title: Obtain Medical Verification and the Notification of Death (Form DHA-1663 / BI-1663)
steps.html:
The initial procedure depends on whether the death resulted from natural causes under medical care or occurred suddenly or unnaturally [1]:

  • Natural death in a hospital, care facility, or at home: When a person dies of natural causes in a hospital or clinic, or at home under the care of a registered medical practitioner who is satisfied that the death was natural, the attending doctor (or authorized professional nurse where applicable) examines the deceased and completes and signs the medical sections of the official Notification / Register of Death / Stillbirth (Form DHA-1663, formerly BI-1663) [1].
  • Unnatural, sudden, or unexplained death outside a hospital: If the death occurred suddenly at home without a treating doctor able to certify natural causes, in a public place, or from an accident or unnatural cause, call the South African Police Service (SAPS emergency phone: 10111) immediately [1]. Do not move the body before police arrive. SAPS opens an inquest docket and arranges for the provincial Department of Health Forensic Pathology Service to transfer the deceased to a state medico-legal mortuary for a statutory post-mortem examination under the Inquests Act [1]. Once the forensic pathologist completes the autopsy, the forensic medical officer completes the medical section of Form DHA-1663 so the family's appointed funeral undertaker can collect the deceased [1].

steps.title: Check Funeral Policies and Appoint a Designated Funeral Undertaker
steps.html:
Before making out-of-pocket commitments, check whether your family member held a funeral insurance policy, bank or retail funeral cover, medical scheme burial benefit, or trade union/employer funeral benefit (many South African funeral policies pay out within 24 to 48 hours of receiving the Death Certificate and DHA-1663/BI-1680) [1].

  • Requirement for a designated funeral undertaker: Under the Births and Deaths Registration Act, the informant and a registered funeral undertaker holding a valid municipal Certificate of Competence and Department of Home Affairs designation number must complete their respective sections of Form DHA-1663 to obtain a Burial Order [1]. You can verify or locate an accredited funeral provider through the National Funeral Directors Association of South Africa (email: info@nfda.org.za) [3]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual funeral providers.
  • Burial and cremation permits: No burial or cremation may legally take place in South Africa until the Department of Home Affairs has issued the Burial Order (Form BI-14 / DHA-14), and for cremations, the additional statutory medical referee cremation certificates required by provincial cremation regulations have been signed [1].

steps.title: Register the Death with the Department of Home Affairs (DHA)
steps.html:
Your appointed funeral undertaker normally assists the family informant in submitting the completed Form DHA-1663 (sealed medical cause-of-death page plus demographic pages), the deceased's original South African barcoded ID book or Smart ID card (or passport), and a certified copy of the informant's ID to the local office of the Department of Home Affairs (Contact Centre phone: 0800 60 11 90) or an on-site DHA hospital registration desk [1]:

  • Burial Order (Form BI-14) and Death Certificate: Upon registering the death on the National Population Register, the Department of Home Affairs issues the Death Report (Form BI-1680), the Burial Order (Form BI-14) required by the cemetery or crematorium, and an abridged Death Certificate free of charge on the day of registration (you can also apply for an unabridged Death Certificate where needed for foreign assets or cross-border matters) [1].
  • If a South African citizen dies abroad: When a death occurs outside South Africa, report it to the nearest South African Embassy or Consulate or the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO Consular Section in Pretoria, phone: +27 12 351 1000) so the foreign death certificate can be transmitted to the Department of Home Affairs in Pretoria [1][4].

steps.title: Claim Statutory UIF Death Benefits, SASSA, and Survivor Pensions
steps.html:
Once you have the official Death Certificate and Death Report (BI-1680), notify social security and pension bodies promptly [1][5]:

  • Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) Death Benefits: If your family member was employed and contributed to the UIF, surviving dependants (a surviving spouse or life partner, or dependent children under 21, or up to 25 if full-time learners, or disabled children) can claim UIF Dependant's / Death Benefits through the Department of Employment and Labour (UIF call centre phone: 0800 030 007) at a local Labour Centre or via uFiling [5]. Submit Form UI-2.5 (or UI-2.6 for children), the employer's Form UI-19 and salary schedule (UI-2.7), bank confirmation Form UI-2.8, certified copies of the Death Certificate, the deceased's and claimant's IDs, and marriage/birth certificates within 18 months of the death [5].
  • South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) and occupational pensions: If the deceased received a SASSA older person's, disability, or war veteran's grant, report the death to SASSA (phone: 0800 60 10 11; DHA registration also updates the population register) so grants are stopped [1]. If the deceased belonged to the Government Employees Pension Fund (GEPF, phone: 0800 117 669) or a private retirement fund, contact the fund administrator regarding funeral benefits, spouse's/orphan's pensions, and Section 37C death benefit distributions [1].

steps.title: Report the Deceased Estate to the Master of the High Court (Within 14 Days) and Notify SARS and Banks
steps.html:
Under Section 7 of the Administration of Estates Act 66 of 1965, every deceased estate in South Africa with any assets must be reported to the Master of the High Court within 14 days of the date of death [2][6]:

  • Reporting the estate (Form J294) and threshold at R250,000: Report the estate either online via the Department of Justice Deceased Estate Online Registration portal or at the Master of the High Court office (or designated Magistrate's Court service point for smaller estates) in the jurisdiction where the deceased ordinarily resided [2][6][7]. Submit the Death Notice (Form J294), original or certified Death Certificate, original Will (if any), Next-of-Kin Affidavit (Form J192 if intestate), Inventory of assets (Form J243), and Marriage Certificate or declaration of marital regime [2][6].
    • Estates valued at R250,000 or less (Section 18(3)): You also submit the Undertaking and Acceptance of Master's Directions (Form J155), and the Master issues Letters of Authority, enabling the appointed representative to administer and distribute the estate without a full Liquidation and Distribution Account [2][6].
    • Estates valued above R250,000: You submit the Acceptance of Trust as Executor (Form J190), and the Master issues Letters of Executorship; for complex or higher-value estates, appointing an attorney, trust company, or chartered accountant as agent is usually required to prepare the formal Liquidation and Distribution Account [2][6].
  • Notifying banks and insurers: Banks in South Africa freeze the deceased's sole accounts upon notification of death (though they may allow limited release toward verified funeral expenses before Letters of Executorship or Authority are issued). Once the Master issues Letters of Executorship or Letters of Authority, present them to banks and life insurers to collect estate funds [2][6].
  • Tax compliance with the South African Revenue Service (SARS): The executor or authorized representative must notify the South African Revenue Service (phone: 0800 00 7277 or via SARS eFiling / online query system) to code the profile as a deceased estate, submit income tax returns up to the date of death, manage any post-death estate tax or Estate Duty (Form REV267 for dutiable estates above the R3.5 million abatement), and obtain the SARS Deceased Estate Compliance (DEC) letter required by the Master of the High Court before final winding up [8][9].

closingQuestion: To help us point you to the exact Master of the High Court office and applicable forms, in which South African province and city did your family member reside, and is the gross value of the estate above or below R250,000?

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in India: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in India: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in India: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are sorry for your loss. When a family member dies in India, the immediate medical, funeral, civil registration, and financial steps follow national statutory rules alongside municipal or panchayat procedures. Here is the five-step sequence to handle each stage clearly.

steps.title: Medical verification and official certification of death
steps.html:
The first requirement is an official medical certification of the cause of death under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 [1][2]:

  • Death in a hospital or nursing facility: The attending hospital physician verifies the death and issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death on Form 4 (for institutional in-patient deaths), which is required before the hospital mortuary releases the body and before civil registration can proceed [1][2].
  • Natural death at home: If the deceased was under the care of a registered medical practitioner (RMP), call that physician to examine the body and issue the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death on Form 4A (for non-institutional deaths) [1][2].
  • Sudden, accidental, or unattended death outside a hospital: Do not move the body. Call the national emergency response number 112 so the local police can attend, record a First Information Report (FIR) or inquest report under Section 194 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (formerly Section 174 CrPC), and arrange a post-mortem examination at an authorised government hospital before issuing a police No Objection Certificate (NOC) for cremation or burial [2].

steps.title: Checking funeral pre-arrangements and appointing an authorised provider
steps.html:
Check whether your family member held a pre-arranged funeral plan, employer medical/welfare cover, or repatriation policy before making independent commitments. In India, burial or cremation is normally carried out promptly (often within 24 hours for natural deaths, or once the post-mortem and police clearance are completed), unless the body is placed in an authorised hospital or municipal mortuary freezer while relatives travel:

  • Local cremation or burial: The family or an appointed local funeral provider books a slot at the municipal crematorium, burial ground, or cemetery (such as facilities managed by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation, Municipal Corporation of Delhi, or local Nagar Palika / Gram Panchayat) by presenting the doctor's Form 4 or Form 4A (plus the police NOC in medico-legal cases) and the deceased's identity document (such as an Aadhaar card) [1][2].
  • Domestic or cross-border transport: If the remains must be transported to another state or abroad, appoint an experienced funeral and mortuary service to arrange embalming, a coffin sealing certificate, and public health clearance.

steps.title: Registering the death with the civil registry within 21 days
steps.html:
Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, every death must be registered with the local Registrar of Births and Deaths (Municipal Corporation, Municipality, or Gram Panchayat) for the jurisdiction where the death occurred within 21 days [1][2]:

  • Who reports the death: For a hospital death, the medical institution normally transmits the institutional death report and Form 4 directly to the local Registrar, after which the family collects or downloads the official Death Certificate [1][2]. For a death at home, the head of the household or closest relative submits the report (Form 2), the doctor's Form 4A, and the cremation or burial ground receipt through the Civil Registration System (CRS) portal or at the municipal citizen service centre [1][2].
  • Late registration: Registration within 21 days is free of statutory late penalty; registration between 21 and 30 days requires a late fee and registrar permission, between 30 days and 1 year requires written permission from the designated higher authority and an affidavit, and after 1 year requires an order from an Executive Magistrate [2].
  • Certificates and identity updates: Obtain multiple certified copies (or digitally signed CRS copies) of the official Death Certificate [1]. In India, civil registration does not automatically close bank accounts, pensions, or tax profiles, so the family must notify each institution directly.

steps.title: Claiming funeral grants, survivor pensions, and social security benefits
steps.html:
Depending on the deceased's employment and insurance history, eligible nominees or surviving family members can apply for statutory benefits:

  • Employees' Provident Fund Organisation: If the deceased contributed to the EPF, the registered nominee or legal heirs submit the unified Composite Claim Form in Death Cases (which combines Form 20 for the final Provident Fund balance, Form 10D for the Employees' Pension Scheme monthly survivor pension, and Form 5IF for the Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance lump-sum assurance payout) online via the Member e-Sewa portal or through the last employer to the regional office of the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (toll-free helpline 14470 or 1800-118-005) [3].
  • Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC): If the deceased was an insured worker under the ESI scheme, the eldest surviving family member or the person who paid for the funeral can claim lump-sum ESIC Funeral Expenses (up to INR 15,000 to INR 20,000 under applicable rules) using ESIC Form 22 [4], and eligible dependants can claim monthly Dependants' Benefit if death resulted from an employment injury.
  • Overseas migrant workers (PBBY): If the deceased worked abroad under the Emigration Check Required (ECR) framework and held cover under the Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana, accidental death and repatriation claims (up to INR 10 lakh sum insured) are filed through the insurer and the Ministry of External Affairs eMigrate framework [5].

steps.title: Notifying banks, insurers, and tax authorities and completing estate succession
steps.html:
To settle the estate, transfer assets, and complete tax compliance:

  • Legal Heir Certificate, Succession Certificate, or Probate: Apply to the local Tehsildar, Talukdar, or Revenue Officer (often via the state e-District portal) for a Legal Heir Certificate (or Surviving Member Certificate) to handle routine pension, employer, and utility transfers. If the deceased held financial assets (such as bank deposits or securities) without a registered nominee and without a will, apply to the competent Civil Court for a Succession Certificate under the Indian Succession Act, 1925. If the deceased left a will, confirm whether formal court Probate or Letters of Administration are mandatory in the relevant high court / presidency jurisdiction.
  • Banks and life insurers: Notify each bank and life insurer (such as LIC or private insurers) with the Death Certificate, KYC documents, and either the registered nomination claim form or the Legal Heir / Succession Certificate.
  • Income Tax compliance: The legal heir or executor must register as a Representative Assessee on the e-Filing portal of the Income Tax Department (national helpline 1800-103-0025 or 1800-419-0025) by uploading the Death Certificate, the PAN cards of both the deceased and the legal heir, and the Legal Heir or Succession Certificate, in order to file the final income tax return for the period up to the date of death [6]. India does not levy a separate inheritance or estate tax.

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Philippines: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Philippines: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in Philippines: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are sorry for your loss. When a family member dies in the Philippines, the immediate medical, funeral, civil registry, and estate procedures follow national health, civil registration, and tax rules alongside local city or municipal steps. Here is the five-step sequence to navigate each stage.

steps.title: Medical verification and official certification of death
steps.html:
Every death in the Philippines must be medically certified on Municipal Form No. 103 (Certificate of Death) before embalming, burial, cremation, or civil registration can proceed [1]:

  • Death in a hospital or care facility: The attending hospital physician examines the deceased and completes the medical certification section of Municipal Form No. 103 [1].
  • Natural death at home: Report the death immediately to the Barangay and the local Municipal Health Officer (MHO) or City Health Officer (CHO) (or the attending physician, if the person was under active medical care). The MHO or CHO examines the body, certifies the cause of death, and signs the review section of Municipal Form No. 103 [1].
  • Sudden, accidental, or medico-legal death outside a hospital: Do not move or embalm the body. Call the national emergency hotline 911 or the local Philippine National Police (PNP) station so medico-legal officers (PNP Forensic Group or National Bureau of Investigation) can conduct an investigation or autopsy and issue the medico-legal clearance required for the Certificate of Death [1].

steps.title: Checking funeral pre-arrangements and appointing a licensed funeral provider
steps.html:
Check whether your family member held a pre-need memorial plan, HMO/life insurance policy, or employer assistance before signing a service contract:

  • Appointing a licensed provider: Engage a funeral establishment and mortuary licensed by the Department of Health (DOH) and accredited by the local government unit. The funeral provider coordinates the retrieval of the body, embalming or refrigeration, and preparation of Municipal Form No. 103 for filing [1].
  • Statutory 48-hour sanitation rule: Under Presidential Decree No. 856 (Code on Sanitation of the Philippines), remains that are not embalmed must generally be buried or cremated within 48 hours after death (or within 12 hours if death resulted from a dangerous communicable disease), unless properly embalmed by a DOH-licensed embalmer or preserved in an authorised mortuary.

steps.title: Registering the death with the Local Civil Registrar within 30 days
steps.html:
Under Philippine civil registration laws (Act No. 3753), the death must be registered within 30 days from the date of death at the Local Civil Registry Office (LCRO) of the city or municipality where the death occurred [1]:

  • How registration and permits work: The informant (nearest relative) or the authorised funeral provider submits four copies of Municipal Form No. 103, signed by the attending physician and reviewed by the local Health Officer, to the LCRO [1]. At the same time, you obtain the Burial Permit or Cremation Permit (and a Transfer Permit if the body is moving to another municipality) from the local health/civil registry office before interment or cremation [1].
  • Obtaining PSA Security Paper (SECPA) copies: Once registered at the LCRO, the record is transmitted to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). Because standard PSA batch transmission can take several weeks or months, ask the LCRO for Advance Transmittal if you need an official PSA Death Certificate printed on Security Paper (SECPA) urgently for benefit or estate claims, and keep multiple LCRO-certified true copies for immediate notifications [1][2][3]. Civil registration does not automatically notify banks, pension bodies, or the tax authority.

steps.title: Claiming statutory funeral grants, survivor pensions, and death benefits
steps.html:
Depending on whether the deceased worked in the private sector, government service, or overseas, eligible family members or the person who paid the funeral bill can claim statutory benefits:

  • Social Security System: For private-sector, self-employed, or voluntary members, the person who shouldered the funeral costs can file a Funeral Benefit claim (ranging from PHP 20,000 to PHP 60,000 depending on contributions) with the official funeral receipt and Death Certificate [2], while primary beneficiaries (legal spouse and dependent minor/incapacitated children) or secondary beneficiaries can claim the Death Benefit (monthly survivorship pension if at least 36 monthly contributions were paid, or a lump sum otherwise) via the My.SSS portal or any branch of the Social Security System (hotline 1455 or +63 2 81455) [3].
  • Government Service Insurance System: If the deceased was a government employee or pensioner, the person who paid the funeral expenses can claim the GSIS Funeral Benefit (PHP 50,000 under current rules) [4], and eligible primary beneficiaries can apply for the Survivorship Benefit through the Government Service Insurance System (contact centre 8847-4747) [5].
  • Pag-IBIG Fund, PhilHealth, and OWWA: Legal heirs can also claim the deceased member's Total Accumulated Value (TAV) savings and additional death benefit from the Pag-IBIG Fund (HDMF), settle inpatient hospital coverage deductions with PhilHealth prior to hospital discharge, and, for active or non-active Overseas Filipino Workers, apply to the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) for death and burial assistance (up to PHP 100,000 to PHP 200,000 plus PHP 20,000 burial benefit for active OWWA members).

steps.title: Notifying banks, insurers, and the BIR and completing estate settlement
steps.html:
To unlock bank accounts, transfer real property or vehicles, and settle tax obligations in the Philippines:

  • BIR Estate Tax Return within 1 year: Under the National Internal Revenue Code (as amended by the TRAIN Law), the heirs, executor, or administrator must file the Estate Tax Return (BIR Form 1801) with the Bureau of Internal Revenue (Revenue District Office where the deceased was domiciled, customer assistance +63 2 8538-3200) within one (1) year from the date of death, paying the flat 6% estate tax on the net estate after statutory deductions (including the PHP 5,000,000 standard deduction and up to PHP 10,000,000 family home deduction) to obtain the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR) [6][7].
  • Extrajudicial Settlement vs. Judicial Probate: If the deceased left no will and no unpaid debts, and all heirs are of legal age (or duly represented), the heirs may execute a notarised Deed of Extrajudicial Settlement of Estate (or an Affidavit of Self-Adjudication if there is only one sole heir), which must be published once a week for three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation [6]. If the deceased left a will, a petition for Probate of Will must be filed with the Regional Trial Court.
  • Banks and private insurers: Notify banks promptly upon death; note that under BIR rules, banks may allow withdrawals from the deceased's deposit accounts subject to a 6% final withholding tax (unless exempted via BIR certification) prior to issuing the eCAR [6][7].

title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Singapore: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Singapore: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist in Singapore: medical death certification and coroner/police clearance, appointing a licensed funeral director, civil death registration and statutory deadlines, pension and survivor benefit claims, and estate probate, tax filings, and bank notifications.
introHtml: We are sorry for your loss. Singapore uses an integrated digital process for medical death certification, automatic civil registration, and government bereavement notifications. Here are the five official steps to handle immediate arrangements, benefits, and estate administration.

steps.title: Medical verification and official certification of death
steps.html:
A registered medical practitioner or the State Coroner must certify the cause of death before a funeral or cremation can take place [1][2]:

  • Death in a hospital or nursing facility: The attending ward doctor examines the person and digitally certifies the Certificate of Cause of Death (CCOD) online [1][2].
  • Expected natural death at home: Contact the deceased's regular family doctor or a house-call doctor to visit the home, verify the death, and submit the digital CCOD online (bring the deceased's NRIC or passport and medical records) [2].
  • Sudden, unnatural, or unattended death outside a hospital: If the doctor cannot determine the cause of death or the death was sudden or accidental, call the Singapore Police Force at 999 (or emergency ambulance 995). The police will arrange for the Police Hearse to transfer the body to the Health Sciences Authority Forensic Medicine Division (Mortuary@HSA, located at Block 9, Singapore General Hospital, Outram Road, phone +65 6222 1712) [2][3]. Next of kin attend Mortuary@HSA the following morning with the deceased's and their own identification so the State Coroner can review the case, determine whether an autopsy is needed, and issue the CCOD and release order [2][3].

steps.title: Checking pre-arrangements and appointing a licensed funeral director
steps.html:
Check whether your family member made pre-planned funeral wishes or held a funeral/life insurance policy, then appoint a licensed funeral director:

  • Appointing a funeral director: You can locate a licensed provider through the Association of Funeral Directors Singapore directory [4]. Once engaged, the funeral director collects the body from the home, hospital mortuary, or Mortuary@HSA, arranges embalming (if desired) and coffining, and coordinates wake venues (such as an HDB void deck via the Town Council, a funeral parlour, or landed property with applicable road permits) [2][4].
  • Booking cremation or burial with the NEA: Using the digital CCOD or Death Certificate, you or your appointed funeral director apply online through the National Environment Agency ePortal (contact centre +65 6225 5632) for a Permit to Bury/Cremate and book a cremation slot at Mandai Crematorium or a burial plot at Choa Chu Kang Cemetery [2].

steps.title: Downloading the Digital Death Certificate via MyLegacy@LifeSG
steps.html:
In Singapore, physical registration at an Immigration & Checkpoints Authority counter or police post is no longer required for domestic deaths [1][2]:

  • Automatic registration within 24 hours: As soon as the doctor or Coroner submits the CCOD online, the death is automatically registered with the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority [1][3].
  • 30-day download deadline on MyLegacy: The next of kin must visit the MyLegacy@LifeSG portal within 30 days of the certification of death to download and save the official Digital Death Certificate (using the Death Document Number, the deceased's NRIC/FIN or passport number, and date of death) [1][3]. Download and store multiple digital and printed copies immediately; after 30 days, retrieving a Death Extract from ICA requires a formal application and fee [1][3].
  • Automatic agency notification: Once registered with ICA, the death is automatically shared with core Singapore government agencies (including the CPF Board, IRAS, HDB, and the Public Trustee's Office), invalidating the deceased's NRIC and Singpass [1][5][7].

steps.title: Claiming CPF nomination payouts and small-estate funds
steps.html:
Statutory retirement and social security balances in Singapore are settled through the Central Provident Fund and the Ministry of Law:

  • Central Provident Fund (CPF) balances and Dependants' Protection Scheme (DPS): Because the Central Provident Fund Board (helpline +65 6227 1188) is notified automatically of the death, you do not need to register the death with CPF if the deceased held a Singapore NRIC [5]. If the deceased made a valid CPF Nomination, the CPF Board contacts the nominated beneficiaries directly within about 10 working days and automatically disburses the savings to eligible adult SC/PR nominees' bank accounts [5]. If the deceased was insured under the Dependants' Protection Scheme (DPS), contact the designated insurer (Great Eastern Life) to claim the term life payout.
  • Un-nominated CPF monies and small estates (up to SGD 50,000): If the deceased did not make a valid CPF nomination, CPF transfers the remaining savings to the Public Trustee's Office (under the Ministry of Law, helpline 1800-225-5529) for distribution under Singapore's Intestate Succession Act (or the Administration of Muslim Law Act for Muslim estates) [5][6]. The Public Trustee's Office can also administer other un-nominated estate assets (such as bank accounts, shares, or insurance policies) without a court order if the total value of the non-CPF estate does not exceed SGD 50,000 and no court grant has been filed [6].

steps.title: Completing court probate, tax clearance, and bank notifications
steps.html:
For estates exceeding SGD 50,000 or involving real property (such as an HDB flat or private property):

  • Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration: If the deceased left a valid will, the named executor applies to the Family Justice Courts (or the Syariah Court for Muslim inheritance certificates) for a Grant of Probate; if there is no will, the eligible next of kin applies for Letters of Administration via the Singapore Courts Probate eService [7].
  • Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS): Although Singapore abolished estate duty for deaths on or after 15 February 2008, the executor or legal personal representative remains responsible for settling the deceased's income tax up to the date of death (and any estate income tax if assets continue generating income during administration) with the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (helpline 1800-356-8300) [8].
  • Banks, insurers, and HDB: Present the Digital Death Certificate (and the Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration once issued) to each commercial bank, private insurer, and the Housing & Development Board (HDB) to close or transfer accounts and update flat ownership [2][7].
