title: Cross-Border Terminal Illness & Advance Care Checklist: Switzerland & France
titleEn: Cross-Border Terminal Illness & Advance Care Checklist: Switzerland & France
cardSummary: Official 5-step guide for terminal illness and advance care planning across Switzerland and France: palliative/hospice care and cross-border healthcare coverage, advance directives in both jurisdictions, separate medical and financial powers of attorney, caregiver leave & disability benefits, and cross-border wills & estate planning.
introHtml: When your family member is diagnosed with a serious, life-limiting, or terminal illness and has ties through residence, citizenship, family, or assets across both Switzerland and France, medical, legal, and financial advance care documents should be coordinated early in both jurisdictions. Because advance directives, lasting powers of attorney, social security entitlements, and succession procedures in Switzerland and France are governed by distinct statutory formalities, it is essential to initiate these steps while the ill person retains full decision-making and legal capacity [1][3][4].

steps.title: Organize Palliative and Hospice Care in Switzerland and France and Coordinate Cross-Border Health Insurance
steps.html:
First, ask the attending medical team or hospital social service to establish an interdisciplinary treatment and palliative care plan, and clarify with the competent health insurer whether care will be provided in Switzerland, in France, or across the border [1][2].

  • Palliative Care and Spitex in Switzerland: Under the guidelines of the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (Bundesamt für Gesundheit, phone: +41 58 462 21 11) and the Healthcare Benefits Ordinance (Krankenpflege-Leistungsverordnung - KLV), mandatory basic health insurance (obligatorische Krankenpflegeversicherung - OKP) covers medically prescribed outpatient palliative nursing at home through specialized Spitex services as well as inpatient palliative care wards (subject to the annual deductible and co-payment) [1]. Regional palliative networks, mobile palliative care teams, and inpatient hospices across the cantons (such as Zurich, Geneva, Basel, or Bern) can be accessed via the Swiss Association for Palliative Medicine, Care and Support (palliative.ch - Schweizerische Gesellschaft für Palliative Medizin, Pflege und Begleitung) [1].
  • Palliative Care Structures in France and 100% Cost Coverage (ALD): In France, palliative care is delivered at home through hospital-at-home services (Hospitalisation à domicile - HAD) and mobile palliative care teams (équipes mobiles de soins palliatifs - EMSP), or on an inpatient basis in specialized palliative care units (unités de soins palliatifs - USP) [2]. Guidance on care structures is available from the French National Center for Palliative and End-of-Life Care (Centre national des soins palliatifs et de la fin de vie, phone: +33 1 53 72 33 04) and the French Society for Accompaniment and Palliative Care (Société Française d'Accompagnement et de Soins Palliatifs - SFAP) [2]. Clarvia provides directory information solely for orientation and does not endorse or rate individual providers. For severe, progressive illnesses, the attending physician in France applies for recognition as a long-term illness (Affection de Longue Durée - ALD) with the French statutory health insurance fund (Assurance Maladie, phone from France: 36 46; from abroad: +33 1 84 90 36 46), which covers illness-related medical costs at 100% of the statutory tariff [2][9]. If a transfer of care or cross-border commuter (frontalier) arrangement between Switzerland and France is planned, obtain form S1 (residence in the neighboring country) or prior authorization form S2 (planned treatment in the other state) from the health insurer in advance [1][9].

steps.title: Execute Legally Valid Written Advance Directives in Switzerland and France While Full Capacity Remains
steps.html:
To ensure that end-of-life medical decisions are respected without delay in both countries, the ill person should put their treatment wishes in writing according to each country's national requirements [3][4].

  • Advance Directive in Switzerland (Art. 370 et seq. ZGB): Any person with decision-making capacity may, pursuant to Articles 370 et seq. of the Swiss Civil Code (Zivilgesetzbuch - ZGB), specify in a written, dated, and personally signed advance directive (Patientenverfügung) which medical measures they consent to or refuse in the event of incapacity, and designate a natural person as their healthcare representative [3]. Official guidance is published on the Swiss authorities' information portal (Schweizer Portal ch.ch); recognized template forms are provided, among others, by the Swiss Medical Association (Verbindung der Schweizer Ärztinnen und Ärzte - FMH) and the Swiss Red Cross (Schweizerisches Rotes Kreuz - SRK) [1][3]. The advance directive should be handed to the family doctor or care team and uploaded to the Electronic Patient Record (Elektronisches Patientendossier - EPD); its storage location can also be recorded on the health insurance card [1][3].
  • Advance Directives and Trusted Person in France (Loi Claeys-Leonetti): For medical care in France, the ill person should draw up, date, and sign written advance directives (directives anticipées) and designate in writing a healthcare trusted person (personne de confiance), whose testimony takes priority when consulted by the medical team if the patient can no longer express their wishes [2][4]. The forms can be completed using the official template of the French Ministry of Health and stored in the digital health space (Mon espace santé) as well as in the medical file of the attending French hospital or general practitioner [4].

steps.title: Establish Separate Financial, Care, and Representation Powers of Attorney in Switzerland and France
steps.html:
A foreign power of attorney is often not readily accepted by banks, land registries, or adult protection authorities in the other country. Execute separate instruments in both jurisdictions while full decision-making and legal capacity remains [3][5]:

  • Advance Care Mandate (Art. 360 et seq. ZGB) and Bank Proxies in Switzerland: To cover personal care, financial management, and legal representation in the event of incapacity, a Swiss advance care mandate (Vorsorgeauftrag under Art. 360 et seq. ZGB) must either be handwritten in its entirety from beginning to end, dated, and signed (eigenhändiger Vorsorgeauftrag) or be publicly notarized (öffentlich beurkundet) by a notary [3]. The storage location of the Vorsorgeauftrag can be recorded with the civil registry office in the civil status register (Infostar); if incapacity occurs, the competent Child and Adult Protection Authority (Kindes- und Erwachsenenschutzbehörde - KESB, or in the Canton of Geneva the Tribunal de protection de l'adulte et de l'enfant) examines and validates the document and issues a certificate of representation to the appointed representative [3]. In addition, the ill person should sign dedicated bank powers of attorney directly with their Swiss banks (explicitly valid beyond death if desired), as banks frequently require their own internal forms for ongoing payment transactions [3].
  • Future Protection Mandate (Mandat de protection future) and Bank Proxies in France: For assets, real estate, or legal affairs in France, a future protection mandate (mandat de protection future) under French law can be executed either as a private deed (sous seing privé, countersigned or registered with the tax office) or as a notarial deed (mandat notarié) through the professional body of French notaries (Notaires de France, phone: +33 1 44 90 30 00) [5]. A notarized mandate is particularly necessary if the representative may later need to carry out major acts of disposition such as selling real estate without court guardianship proceedings (tutelle) [5]. In parallel, explicit account powers of attorney (procurations bancaires) should be set up directly with the French banks holding the accounts [5].

steps.title: Claim Statutory Caregiver Leave, Care Allowances, and Severe Illness Benefits
steps.html:
Both Swiss and French law provide financial assistance and statutory leave from work for seriously ill individuals and family caregivers [6][7]:

  • Caregiver Leave and Helplessness Allowance in Switzerland: Working relatives employed under the Swiss Code of Obligations (Obligationenrecht - OR) are entitled to paid short-term leave of up to 3 days per event and up to 10 days per year to care for a family member with a health impairment (Art. 329g OR; for seriously ill minor children, up to 14 weeks of paid care leave is available through the Loss of Earnings Compensation scheme under Art. 329i OR) [6]. If the ill person permanently requires third-party assistance or personal supervision for everyday activities, an income-independent helplessness allowance (Hilflosenentschädigung) under the AHV or IV can be claimed from the cantonal IV office or compensation office; official information leaflets are provided by the AHV/IV Information Center (Informationsstelle AHV/IV) [6]. In addition, cantons and non-profit organizations (such as the Cantonal Cancer League or the Swiss Red Cross) offer respite services for family caregivers [1][6].
  • Family Solidarity Leave (Congé de solidarité familiale), Daily Accompaniment Allowance (AJAP), and Autonomy Allowance (APA) in France: Employees in France who accompany a close relative in an advanced or terminal stage of illness may request statutory family solidarity leave (congé de solidarité familiale) from their employer for up to 3 months (renewable once) or on a part-time basis [7]. During this leave, the Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie (CPAM) under Assurance Maladie pays, upon application, the Daily End-of-Life Accompaniment Allowance (Allocation journalière d'accompagnement d'une personne en fin de vie - AJAP) for up to 21 days (or 42 days if taken part-time) [7]. For ill persons aged 60 or over residing in France, an emergency Personal Autonomy Allowance (Allocation personnalisée d'autonomie - APA en urgence) can also be requested from the departmental council (Conseil départemental) [7].

steps.title: Align Wills, Beneficiary Designations, Bank Access, and Funeral or Repatriation Wishes Between Switzerland and France
steps.html:
Because cross-border estates engage both Swiss succession law (ZGB) and French succession law alongside the EU Succession Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 650/2012, under which Switzerland is treated as a third state), early alignment prevents duplicate proceedings and frozen bank accounts [3][5][8][9]:

  • Pension Funds, AHV Survivor Pensions, and Probate in Switzerland: Review in advance the regulations of the ill person's Swiss occupational pension fund (Pensionskasse / 2nd pillar) and tied private pension (Säule 3a), and submit a written beneficiary designation (Begünstigtenordnung) to the institution if needed, as 2nd and 3rd pillar benefits are paid directly to designated beneficiaries outside the probate estate [3][8]. Following a death, survivors register claims for widow's, widower's, or orphan's pensions with the competent cantonal compensation office or, where residence or cross-border ties are abroad, with the Central Compensation Office (Zentrale Ausgleichsstelle, phone: +41 58 461 91 11) [8]. For the Swiss estate, the competent cantonal inheritance office (Erbschaftsamt) or district court (Bezirksgericht, or a notary depending on the canton) issues the certificate of inheritance (Erbenbescheinigung); note the statutory deadline of 3 months from learning of the death to renounce (Ausschlagung) an over-indebted estate under Art. 566 et seq. ZGB [3].
  • Lump-Sum Death Grant, Survivor Pensions, and Notarial Estate Settlement in France: If the deceased was insured under the French social security system, eligible survivors can apply to the Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie via Assurance Maladie for the lump-sum death benefit (capital décès) and to the basic pension fund (Assurance Retraite / CNAV) and supplementary pension fund (Agirc-Arrco) for a survivor pension (pension de réversion) [9]. Where assets or the last habitual residence are in France, estate settlement (règlement de la succession, including drafting the deed of heirship, acte de notoriété) is handled by a French notary belonging to Notaires de France; the French inheritance tax return (déclaration de succession) must be filed with the tax authorities within 6 months if the death occurred in France, or within 12 months if the death occurred outside France (for example in Switzerland) [5][9]. Finally, record in writing whether local burial or cremation in Switzerland or repatriation to France is desired, so that a licensed funeral director can apply for the international laissez-passer for a corpse (laissez-passer mortuaire) without delay when death occurs [1][5].

closingQuestion: To identify the exact cantonal and departmental authorities for your situation: in which Swiss canton and in which French department are residence or assets located, and in which of the two countries is your family member's primary medical treatment currently taking place?

de.title: Schwere Erkrankung & Vorsorge zwischen Schweiz und Frankreich: Offizielle 5-Schritte-Checkliste
de.cardSummary: Offizielle 5-Schritte-Checkliste bei lebensbedrohlicher Erkrankung mit Bezug zu Schweiz und Frankreich: Palliativversorgung, Patientenverfügungen in beiden Ländern, Vorsorgevollmachten, Pflegezeit sowie Nachlass- und Rückführungsplanung.
de.introHtml: Wenn bei Ihrem Familienangehörigen eine schwere, lebensverkürzende oder unheilbare Erkrankung diagnostiziert wurde und Verbindungen durch Wohnsitz, Staatsangehörigkeit, Familie oder Vermögenswerte sowohl zur Schweiz als auch zu Frankreich bestehen, sollten medizinische, rechtliche und finanzielle Vorsorgedokumente frühzeitig in beiden Rechtsordnungen abgestimmt werden. Da Patientenverfügungen, Vorsorgevollmachten, Sozialversicherungsansprüche und Nachlassverfahren in der Schweiz und in Frankreich unterschiedlichen gesetzlichen Formvorschriften unterliegen, ist es entscheidend, diese Schritte einzuleiten, solange die erkrankte Person voll urteils- und geschäftsfähig ist [1][3][4].

steps.title: Palliativ- und Hospizversorgung in der Schweiz und in Frankreich sowie grenzüberschreitende Krankenkassenkoordination organisieren
steps.html:
Bitten Sie zunächst das behandelnde Ärzteteam oder den Spitalsozialdienst, einen interdisziplinären Behandlungs- und Palliativplan zu erstellen, und klären Sie mit dem zuständigen Krankenversicherer, ob die Betreuung in der Schweiz, in Frankreich oder grenzüberschreitend erfolgt [1][2].

  • Palliativversorgung und Spitex in der Schweiz: Gemäss den Vorgaben der zuständigen Bundesbehörde (Bundesamt für Gesundheit, Telefon: +41 58 462 21 11) und der Krankenpflege-Leistungsverordnung (KLV) übernimmt die obligatorische Krankenpflegeversicherung (OKP) nach ärztlicher Anordnung die Kosten für ambulante Palliativpflege zu Hause durch spezialisierte Spitex-Dienste sowie für stationäre Palliativabteilungen (abzüglich Franchise und Selbstbehalt) [1]. Regionale Palliativnetzwerke, mobile Palliativdienste und stationäre Hospize in den Kantonen (beispielsweise in Zürich, Genf, Basel oder Bern) sind über die Fachgesellschaft palliative.ch (Schweizerische Gesellschaft für Palliative Medizin, Pflege und Begleitung) erschlossen [1].
  • Palliativstrukturen in Frankreich und Kostenübernahme (ALD): In Frankreich erfolgt die Palliativversorgung zu Hause über die spitalexterne Komplexbehandlung (Hospitalisation à domicile - HAD) und mobile Palliativteams (équipes mobiles de soins palliatifs - EMSP) oder stationär in spezialisierten Palliativstationen (unités de soins palliatifs - USP) [2]. Orientierung zu den Versorgungsstrukturen bieten das nationale französische Informationszentrum (Centre national des soins palliatifs et de la fin de vie, Telefon: +33 1 53 72 33 04) sowie die Fachgesellschaft Société Française d'Accompagnement et de Soins Palliatifs (SFAP) [2]. Clarvia stellt Verzeichnisinformationen ausschliesslich zur Orientierung bereit und spricht keine Empfehlungen oder Bewertungen einzelner Anbieter aus. Bei schweren, fortschreitenden Erkrankungen beantragt die behandelnde Ärztin oder der behandelnde Arzt in Frankreich die Einstufung als anerkannte Langzeiterkrankung (Affection de Longue Durée - ALD) bei der gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung (Assurance Maladie, Telefon aus Frankreich: 36 46; aus dem Ausland: +33 1 84 90 36 46), wodurch krankheitsbedingte Behandlungskosten zu 100 % des Kassentarifs übernommen werden [2][9]. Bei einem geplanten Behandlungswechsel oder Grenzgängerstatus zwischen der Schweiz und Frankreich sollte vorab über die Krankenversicherung die Bescheinigung S1 (Wohnsitz im Nachbarland) bzw. die vorherige Genehmigung S2 (geplante Behandlung im anderen Staat) eingeholt werden [1][9].

steps.title: Rechtsgültige schriftliche Patientenverfügungen in der Schweiz und in Frankreich bei voller Urteilsfähigkeit erstellen
steps.html:
Damit medizinische Entscheidungen am Lebensende in beiden Ländern ohne Verzögerung respektiert werden, sollte die erkrankte Person ihre Behandlungswünsche nach den jeweiligen nationalen Vorgaben schriftlich festhalten [3][4].

  • Patientenverfügung in der Schweiz (Art. 370 ff. ZGB): Jede urteilsfähige Person kann gemäss Art. 370 ff. des Schweizerischen Zivilgesetzbuches (ZGB) in einer schriftlichen, datierten und eigenhändig unterzeichneten Patientenverfügung festlegen, welchen medizinischen Massnahmen sie im Fall der Urteilsunfähigkeit zustimmt oder welche sie ablehnt, und eine natürliche Person als medizinische Vertretungsperson benennen [3]. Offizielle Hinweise dazu finden sich auf dem Informationsportal der Schweizer Behörden (Schweizer Portal ch.ch); anerkannte Formularvorlagen stellen unter anderem die Verbindung der Schweizer Ärztinnen und Ärzte (FMH) und das Schweizerische Rote Kreuz (SRK) bereit [1][3]. Die Patientenverfügung sollte dem Hausarzt oder Behandlungsteam übergeben und im Elektronischen Patientendossier (EPD) hinterlegt werden; zudem kann der Hinterlegungsort auf der Versichertenkarte eingetragen werden [1][3].
  • Patientenverfügung und Vertrauensperson in Frankreich (Loi Claeys-Leonetti): Für Behandlungen in Frankreich sollte die erkrankte Person schriftliche Patientenverfügungen (directives anticipées) verfassen, datieren und unterzeichnen sowie schriftlich eine medizinische Vertrauensperson (personne de confiance) benennen, die bei Verlust der Äusserungsfähigkeit vom Ärzteteam vorrangig konsultiert wird [2][4]. Die Formulare können nach dem offiziellen Muster des französischen Gesundheitsministeriums erstellt und im digitalen Gesundheitskonto (Mon espace santé) sowie in der Patientenakte des behandelnden französischen Krankenhauses oder Hausarztes hinterlegt werden [4].

steps.title: Getrennte Finanz-, Vorsorge- und Vertretungsvollmachten in der Schweiz und in Frankreich errichten
steps.html:
Eine ausländische Vollmacht wird von Banken, Grundbuchämtern oder Erwachsenenschutzbehörden im jeweils anderen Staat häufig nicht ohne Weiteres akzeptiert. Errichten Sie daher getrennte Urkunden, solange volle Urteils- und Geschäftsfähigkeit besteht [3][5]:

  • Vorsorgeauftrag (Art. 360 ff. ZGB) und Bankvollmachten in der Schweiz: Für die Personensorge, die Vermögenssorge und die Vertretung im Rechtsverkehr bei Urteilsunfähigkeit muss ein Vorsorgeauftrag nach Art. 360 ff. ZGB entweder von Anfang bis Ende vollständig von Hand niedergeschrieben, datiert und unterzeichnet (eigenhändiger Vorsorgeauftrag) oder durch eine Urkundsperson öffentlich beurkundet werden [3]. Der Aufbewahrungsort des Vorsorgeauftrags kann beim Zivilstandsamt im Personenstandsregister (Infostar) eingetragen werden; tritt die Urteilsunfähigkeit ein, prüft und validiert die zuständige Kindes- und Erwachsenenschutzbehörde (KESB, im Kanton Genf das Tribunal de protection de l'adulte et de l'enfant) das Dokument und stellt der beauftragten Person eine Vertretungsurkunde aus [3]. Zusätzlich sollte die erkrankte Person direkt bei ihren Schweizer Banken eigene Bankvollmachten (auf Wunsch ausdrücklich über den Tod hinaus geltend) unterzeichnen, da Banken für den laufenden Zahlungsverkehr oft bankeigene Formulare verlangen [3].
  • Vorsorgevollmacht (Mandat de protection future) und Bankvollmachten in Frankreich: Für Vermögenswerte, Immobilien oder rechtliche Angelegenheiten in Frankreich kann ein Vorsorgeauftrag nach französischem Recht (mandat de protection future) entweder privatschriftlich (sous seing privé, mit Gegenzeichnung oder Registrierung beim Finanzamt) oder als notarielle Urkunde (mandat notarié) über die Berufsorganisation der französischen Notare (Notaires de France, Telefon: +33 1 44 90 30 00) errichtet werden [5]. Ein notarielles Mandat ist insbesondere dann erforderlich, wenn die bevollmächtigte Person später auch weitreichende Verfügungen wie Immobilienverkäufe ohne gerichtliches Betreuungsverfahren (tutelle) vornehmen soll [5]. Parallel dazu sollten direkt bei den französischen kontoführenden Banken ausdrückliche Kontovollmachten (procurations bancaires) eingerichtet werden [5].

steps.title: Gesetzlichen Betreuungsurlaub, Pflegegeld und Sozialleistungen bei schwerer Erkrankung beantragen
steps.html:
Sowohl das schweizerische als auch das französische Recht sehen finanzielle Hilfen und Arbeitsfreistellungen für erkrankte Personen und betreuende Angehörige vor [6][7]:

  • Betreuungsurlaub und Hilflosenentschädigung in der Schweiz: Erwerbstätige Angehörige mit einem Arbeitsvertrag nach schweizerischem Obligationenrecht haben für die kurzfristige Betreuung eines gesundheitlich beeinträchtigten Familienmitglieds Anspruch auf bezahlten Urlaub von bis zu 3 Tagen pro Ereignis und höchstens 10 Tagen pro Jahr (Art. 329g OR; bei schwer kranken minderjährigen Kindern besteht ein bis zu 14-wöchiger Betreuungsurlaub über die Erwerbsersatzordnung nach Art. 329i OR) [6]. Ist die erkrankte Person für alltägliche Lebensverrichtungen dauerhaft auf Hilfe Dritter oder persönliche Überwachung angewiesen, kann bei der kantonalen IV-Stelle bzw. Ausgleichskasse eine einkommensunabhängige Hilflosenentschädigung der AHV oder IV beantragt werden; die offiziellen Merkblätter stellt die Koordinationsstelle (Informationsstelle AHV/IV) bereit [6]. Ergänzend bieten die Kantone und gemeinnützige Organisationen (wie die Kantonale Krebsliga oder das Schweizerische Rote Kreuz) Entlastungsdienste für pflegende Angehörige an [1][6].
  • Begleiturlaub (Congé de solidarité familiale), Begleitgeld (AJAP) und Pflegehilfe (APA) in Frankreich: Arbeitnehmerinnen und Arbeitnehmer in Frankreich, die eine nahestehende Person in einer fortgeschrittenen oder terminalen Krankheitsphase begleiten, können beim Arbeitgeber den gesetzlichen Familienbegleiturlaub (congé de solidarité familiale) für bis zu 3 Monate (einmalig verlängerbar) oder als Teilzeitarbeit beantragen [7]. Während dieses Urlaubs zahlt die Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie (CPAM) im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung (Assurance Maladie) auf Antrag das tägliche Begleitgeld (Allocation journalière d'accompagnement d'une personne en fin de vie - AJAP) für bis zu 21 Tage (bzw. 42 Tage bei Teilzeit) [7]. Für erkrankte Personen ab 60 Jahren mit Wohnsitz in Frankreich kann zudem beim zuständigen Département (Conseil départemental) im Eilverfahren (APA en urgence) die Pflegebeihilfe Allocation personnalisée d'autonomie beantragt werden [7].

steps.title: Testamente, Begünstigtenordnungen, Bankzugang sowie Bestattungs- und Überführungswünsche zwischen der Schweiz und Frankreich abstimmen
steps.html:
Da bei grenzüberschreitenden Sachverhalten sowohl das Schweizer Erbrecht (ZGB) als auch das französische Erbrecht und die EU-Erbrechtsverordnung (Verordnung (EU) Nr. 650/2012, in der die Schweiz als Drittstaat gilt) ineinandergreifen, verhindert eine frühzeitige Abstimmung Doppelverfahren und Kontosperrungen [3][5][8][9]:

  • Vorsorgeeinrichtungen, AHV-Hinterlassenenrenten und Nachlass in der Schweiz: Prüfen Sie vorab das Reglement der Schweizer Pensionskasse (berufliche Vorsorge / 2. Säule) sowie der Gebundenen Selbstvorsorge (Säule 3a) der erkrankten Person und reichen Sie bei Bedarf eine schriftliche Begünstigungserklärung (Begünstigtenordnung) bei der Vorsorgeeinrichtung ein, da Ansprüche aus der 2. und 3. Säule ausserhalb des eigentlichen Nachlasses direkt an die begünstigten Personen ausbezahlt werden [3][8]. Nach einem Todesfall melden die Hinterbliebenen den Leistungsanspruch auf Witwen-, Witwer- oder Waisenrente bei der zuständigen kantonalen Ausgleichskasse oder, bei Wohnsitz oder grenzüberschreitendem Bezug im Ausland, bei der zuständigen Bundesstelle (Zentrale Ausgleichsstelle, Telefon: +41 58 461 91 11) an [8]. Für den Schweizer Nachlass stellt das zuständige kantonale Erbschaftsamt oder Bezirksgericht (bzw. ein Notariat je nach Kanton) die Erbenbescheinigung aus; beachten Sie die gesetzliche Frist von 3 Monaten ab Kenntnis des Todes zur allfälligen Ausschlagung einer überschuldeten Erbschaft nach Art. 566 ff. ZGB [3].
  • Sterbegeld, Hinterbliebenenrenten und notarielle Nachlassabwicklung in Frankreich: War die verstorbene Person im französischen Sozialversicherungssystem versichert, können anspruchsberechtigte Hinterbliebene bei der Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie über die gesetzliche Krankenversicherung (Assurance Maladie) das Sterbegeld (capital décès) sowie bei der Rentenkasse Assurance Retraite (CNAV) und der Zusatzrentenkasse Agirc-Arrco eine Hinterbliebenenrente (pension de réversion) beantragen [9]. Für Vermögenswerte oder einen letzten Wohnsitz in Frankreich wird die Nachlassabwicklung (règlement de la succession, einschliesslich der Erstellung des Erbennachweises acte de notoriété) über ein französisches Notariat der Berufsorganisation (Notaires de France) durchgeführt; die französische Erbschaftssteuererklärung (déclaration de succession) muss beim Finanzamt innerhalb von 6 Monaten bei einem Todesfall in Frankreich bzw. innerhalb von 12 Monaten bei einem Todesfall ausserhalb Frankreichs (etwa in der Schweiz) eingereicht werden [5][9]. Halten Sie schliesslich auch schriftlich fest, ob eine Bestattung oder Kremation in der Schweiz oder eine Überführung nach Frankreich gewünscht wird, damit ein konzessioniertes Bestattungsunternehmen im Todesfall den internationalen Leichenpass (laissez-passer mortuaire) ohne Verzögerung beantragen kann [1][5].

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Mexico Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Mexico Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Mexico dies in United States: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in United States, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Mexico and United States.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. When a citizen or resident of Mexico dies in the United States, medical certification and civil death registration must first be completed under the laws of the U.S. state and county where the death occurred before the Mexican Consulate can issue the consular mortuary transit visa or register the death for legal and pension purposes in Mexico [1][4].

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death and Complete Any County Coroner or Medical Examiner Clearance in the United States
steps.html:
A licensed physician or authorized county forensic official in the United States must certify the cause and manner of death in the state's electronic death registration system before a funeral home can take custody of the body or apply for transit permits [1].

  • Death in a hospital, hospice, or nursing facility: When a person dies under medical care from natural causes, the attending physician or hospital medical staff completes the medical portion of the death certificate and authorizes the release of the body to the family's chosen funeral director [1]. Provide the deceased person's Mexican passport, Matrícula Consular, or voter card (INE) immediately so that full legal names (including both paternal and maternal surnames), date of birth, and nationality match Mexican identity records [4].
  • Sudden, accidental, or unattended death outside a hospital: If the death occurs at a private residence without hospice care, at a workplace, in a hotel, or in public, call 911 immediately. Local police and the county Coroner or Medical Examiner (for example, the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner, the Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences in Texas, or the Cook County Medical Examiner in Illinois) must investigate, determine whether an autopsy is required, and issue forensic clearance before the body is released [1][4].

steps.title: Check Insurance, Appoint Licensed Funeral Providers in the United States and Mexico, and Contact the Mexican Consulate
steps.html:
Before signing an independent funeral contract, verify whether your family member held travel insurance, workplace accident coverage, or a pre-need repatriation policy, and contact the nearest Mexican consulate in the United States [2][4]:

  • Appointing a U.S. funeral director and FTC Funeral Rule protections: You can locate a state-licensed funeral home in the U.S. city of death through the directory of the National Funeral Directors Association (phone: +1 262 789 1880; email: nfda@nfda.org) [3]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific funeral providers. Under the Funeral Rule enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (phone: +1 877 382 4357), every U.S. funeral provider must give the family an itemized General Price List (GPL), allow you to select only the specific goods and services needed (such as direct cremation or international preparation and air shipment), and accept a casket or urn purchased elsewhere without penalty [2].
  • Coordinating with the Mexican Consulate and a receiving funeral home in Mexico: Contact the Protection Department (Departamento de Protección Consular) of the Embassy or Consulate of Mexico in the United States covering the county of death, or call the 24-hour Centro de Información y Asistencia a Personas Mexicanas (CIAM, phone: +1 520 623 7874) operated by the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores [4]. The Mexican Consulate provides a list of local funeral homes experienced in repatriation, explains consular document visa requirements, and evaluates whether families facing severe financial hardship qualify for consular financial assistance toward repatriation or cremation costs [4]. For full-body repatriation, the U.S. funeral director coordinates directly with a sanitary-licensed receiving funeral agency (agencia funeraria autorizada) in the destination municipality in Mexico regulated under the Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios (phone: +52 800 033 5050) and state health authorities (COEPRIS) [4][5].

steps.title: Register the Death with U.S. State Vital Records and Complete Legalization or Consular Registration for Mexico
steps.html:
The appointed U.S. funeral director files the completed death record with the local county registrar or state Vital Records office, which can be located for all 50 states and territories via the National Center for Health Statistics (phone: +1 800 232 4636) Where to Write for Vital Records directory [1].

  • Obtaining certified U.S. Death Certificates and Apostilles: Order multiple certified copies of the official U.S. Death Certificate (including long-form copies showing the cause of death, which are required for Mexican consular clearance and insurance claims) [1][4]. Because both the United States and Mexico are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, any U.S. Death Certificate used directly before courts, banks, or civil registries in Mexico must carry an Apostille issued by the Secretary of State of the U.S. state where the death occurred, accompanied by an official Spanish translation (traducción por perito traductor) [4].
  • Mexican Consular Death Registration (Registro de Defunción) vs. local Registro Civil inscription: Using the certified U.S. Death Certificate and proof of the deceased person's Mexican nationality, the family can register the death directly at the Mexican Consulate in the United States (under the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores) to obtain a Mexican Acta de Defunción valid throughout Mexico [4]. Alternatively, the apostilled and translated U.S. Death Certificate can be inscribed before the local Oficialía o Juzgado del Registro Civil in Mexico so the municipal registrar can issue the Mexican Acta de Defunción and the local Permiso de Inhumación, Cremación o Traslado [4][5].

steps.title: Arrange International Repatriation of Remains or Ashes to Mexico or Local Burial/Cremation in the United States
steps.html:
Your U.S. funeral director and the Mexican Consulate handle the technical mortuary and border-clearance permits depending on whether you choose international repatriation or local disposition [4][5][6]:

  • Repatriation of the body from the United States to Mexico: For air cargo or land-border transport of human remains to Mexico, the U.S. funeral home obtains the state burial-transit permit (permit for disposition of human remains), prepares the body in accordance with sanitary regulations (official embalming Certificate of Embalming, certificate of non-contagious disease signed by the health authority or physician, and placement in a hermetically sealed metal liner inside a shipping casket), and submits the original Death Certificate, Embalming Certificate, and Transit Permit (with Spanish translations) to the Mexican Consulate under the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores [4]. The Mexican Consulate affixes the mandatory consular mortuary visa (visado de certificado de embalsamamiento y permiso de tránsito de cadáveres) free of charge, which is required alongside sanitary clearance under the Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios and Mexican customs at the airport or border port of entry [4][5]. For cross-border movements involving U.S. ports, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (42 CFR 71.55) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection regulate public-health and border documentation [6].
  • Repatriation of cremated ashes or local burial in the United States: If the deceased is cremated in the United States, a family member may transport the cremated ashes to Mexico in airline carry-on luggage in a non-metallic, X-ray-scannable urn [4][6]. To enter Mexico with ashes, present the certified U.S. Death Certificate, the official Certificate of Cremation, and the county health/cremation permit (stamped/visado with Spanish translation via the Mexican Consulate) [4][5]. Families choosing local burial or cremation in the United States need only the state disposition/burial-transit permit arranged by the U.S. funeral home [1][2].

steps.title: Complete Survivor Pension, Funeral Grant, Tax, and Estate Procedures in Mexico and the United States
steps.html:
Once the U.S. Death Certificate (with Apostille) and the Mexican Acta de Defunción are issued, initiate benefit claims and estate administration in both jurisdictions [7][8][9][10]:

  • Social security, retirement funds (AFORE), and succession in Mexico: If the deceased was insured or pensioned under the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (phone from Mexico: 800 623 2323), eligible family members can claim the funeral expense grant (Ayuda para Gastos de Funeral, Trámite IMSS-01-010, equal to two monthly UMA values, claimed within 1 year of death with the funeral invoice and Acta de Defunción) and apply for survivor pensions (Pensión de Viudez, Orfandad o Ascendientes) at the local Unidad de Medicina Familiar (UMF) [7]. Public-sector workers' survivors file equivalent claims with ISSSTE, while individual retirement account balances are claimed from the deceased's AFORE administrator (replaceable via CONSAR / SAR) [7]. For property or bank accounts in Mexico, a Mexican notary public (Notario Público via the Colegio Nacional del Notariado Mexicano) or family court searches the Registro Nacional de Avisos de Testamento (RENAT) and processes the succession (sucesión testamentaria o intestamentaria) [4][7].
  • Social Security, Veterans benefits, final taxes, and Probate in the United States: Report the death to the Social Security Administration (phone: +1 800 772 1213; TTY: +1 800 325 0778; or through the Federal Benefits Unit at the U.S. Embassy/Consulates in Mexico for beneficiaries living in Mexico) to stop monthly payments and apply for the $255 lump-sum death payment and monthly survivor benefits if the deceased earned sufficient U.S. Social Security credits [8]. If the deceased served in the U.S. armed forces, eligible survivors can claim burial allowances and memorial benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs (phone: +1 800 827 1000) using VA Form 21P-530EZ [10]. Finally, the personal representative must file a final federal income tax return (Form 1040, and Form 1310 if claiming a tax refund due to a deceased taxpayer) with the Internal Revenue Service (phone: +1 800 829 1040) and, if the deceased held sole-name U.S. real estate or bank accounts without a Payable-on-Death beneficiary, open estate administration in the local county Probate Court [9].

closingQuestion: To help provide exact state and consular requirements, in which U.S. city and state did the death occur, and to which municipality and state in Mexico would your family like to transport the remains or ashes?

title: What to Do When a Citizen of United States Dies in Canada: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of United States Dies in Canada: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of United States dies in Canada: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in Canada, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in United States and Canada.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. When a citizen or resident of the United States dies in Canada, medical certification and civil death registration must first be completed in the Canadian province or territory where the death occurred before the U.S. Embassy or Consulate can issue the Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad (CRDA) and before remains or cremated ashes are transported across the border to the United States [1][3][4].

steps.title: Obtain the Medical Certificate of Death and Complete Any Provincial Coroner or Medical Examiner Clearance in Canada
steps.html:
Before a funeral provider in Canada can register the death or prepare the body for transport, a qualified medical practitioner or provincial forensic officer must issue the official Medical Certificate of Death (or Bulletin de décès in Quebec) [1].

  • Death in a hospital, hospice, or long-term care facility: When a death occurs under medical supervision from natural causes, the attending physician or nurse practitioner completes and signs the Medical Certificate of Death and releases the body to the appointed funeral home [1]. Provide the deceased person's U.S. passport immediately so their full legal name, date and place of birth, and nationality are recorded accurately for both provincial Vital Statistics and U.S. consular reporting [1][3].
  • Unexpected, accidental, or unattended death outside a hospital: If the death occurs suddenly at a private residence, hotel, or public place, call 911 immediately. Local police and the provincial Coroner or Medical Examiner (such as the Office of the Chief Coroner in Ontario, the BC Coroners Service, the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Alberta, or the Bureau du coroner du Québec) must investigate the circumstances, conduct an autopsy if warranted, and issue the medical release and coroner's certificate before cross-border repatriation or cremation can proceed [1][2].

steps.title: Check Insurance, Appoint Licensed Funeral Directors in Canada and the United States, and Contact the U.S. Embassy or Consulate
steps.html:
Check whether your family member had travel medical insurance, credit-card travel protection, or employer repatriation coverage before signing an independent funeral contract, as an assistance insurer normally coordinates and pays the funeral providers directly [3][4].

  • Appointing a provincially licensed funeral provider in Canada: Funeral homes in Canada are licensed and regulated at the provincial level, such as by the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (phone: +1 647 483 2649; toll-free: +1 844 493 6356; email: info@thebao.ca), Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or provincial associations affiliated with the Funeral Service Association of Canada [1][2]. The Canadian funeral director collects the Medical Certificate of Death, completes the family Statement of Death, registers the death, and coordinates cross-border air or ground transport [1][2].
  • Appointing a receiving funeral home in the United States and contacting the U.S. Consulate: For full-body repatriation to the United States, the Canadian funeral home coordinates with a state-licensed receiving funeral home in the destination U.S. state, which you can locate via the directory of the National Funeral Directors Association (phone: +1 262 789 1880; email: nfda@nfda.org) [5]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific funeral providers. Under the Funeral Rule enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (phone: +1 877 382 4357), the U.S. funeral home must provide an itemized General Price List (GPL) and allow you to select only the receiving and burial services you require [6]. Simultaneously, report the death to the American Citizens Services (ACS) unit at the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Canada (in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Calgary, Halifax, Quebec City, or Winnipeg; or via the U.S. Department of State 24/7 overseas emergency line at +1 888 407 4747 or +1 202 501 4444) [3][4].

steps.title: Register the Death with Provincial Vital Statistics in Canada and Obtain the U.S. Consular Report of Death Abroad (CRDA)
steps.html:
The Canadian funeral director submits the signed Medical Certificate of Death and the Statement of Death to the municipal division registrar or provincial/territorial Vital Statistics office (for example, ServiceOntario and the Office of the Registrar General in Ontario, the Vital Statistics Agency in British Columbia, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) [1].

  • Canadian Funeral Director's Statement of Death vs. Provincial Death Certificate: In most Canadian provinces, the funeral director immediately issues a Funeral Director's Statement of Death (proof of death) for initial administrative steps and obtains the provincial burial or out-of-province transit permit [1][2]. However, you should also order official government-issued Death Certificates (including certified copies showing cause of death where required for insurance or consular files) from the provincial Vital Statistics registry, such as ServiceOntario (phone: +1 800 461 2156 or +1 416 325 8305) [1].
  • U.S. Consular Report of Death Abroad (CRDA, Form DS-2060) and Apostille recognition: Once the official Canadian provincial death certificate is issued, submit it along with the deceased person's U.S. passport to the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in Canada so the consular officer can cancel the passport and issue the official Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad (CRDA, Form DS-2060) to the next of kin or legal representative [3][4]. The CRDA serves in all 50 U.S. states as official English-language proof of death for probate courts, banks, and insurance companies [4]. In addition, because Canada joined the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention in January 2024, Canadian public documents that require direct authentication can receive an Apostille from Global Affairs Canada or the designated provincial ministry (such as Official Documents Services in Ontario or the Ministry of the Attorney General in BC) [1][4].

steps.title: Choose Between International Repatriation of Remains or Ashes to the United States and Local Burial or Cremation in Canada
steps.html:
Your Canadian and U.S. funeral directors coordinate the cross-border health, customs, and mortuary permits across the Canada-U.S. border [7][8]:

  • Repatriation of uncremated human remains from Canada to the United States: Under Memorandum D19-9-3 of the Canada Border Services Agency (phone: +1 800 461 9999; outside Canada: +1 204 983 3500) and the Canadian Quarantine Act, exporting human remains from Canada requires the provincial death certificate or coroner's transit permit, a statement confirming whether the deceased had a communicable disease of concern, and a leak-proof or hermetically sealed shipping container [7]. For entry into the United States by air or land border, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (phone: +1 800 232 4636) human remains importation rules (42 CFR 71.55) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection require an official English death certificate or consular mortuary certificate stating the cause of death, confirmation that the death was not caused by a quarantinable communicable disease (or proof of embalming/hermetic sealing), and the U.S. receiving state's burial-transit permit [3][8].
  • Transporting cremated ashes or choosing local burial/cremation in Canada: Under both Canada Border Services Agency (Memorandum D19-9-3) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines, cremated human remains are exempt from communicable-disease quarantine restrictions [7][8]. A family member can carry cremated ashes into the United States by car or in airline carry-on luggage using an X-ray-scannable non-metallic urn, accompanied by the official Canadian death certificate and the certificate of cremation [3][7][8]. If the family chooses local burial or cremation in Canada, the Canadian funeral director obtains the provincial burial or cremation permit (which requires a Coroner's Cremation Certificate in provinces such as Ontario) [1][2].

steps.title: Complete Survivor Pension, Benefit, Tax, and Probate Steps in the United States and Canada
steps.html:
With the U.S. CRDA (Form DS-2060) and the Canadian provincial Death Certificate, complete post-death benefit claims, tax filings, and estate administration in both countries [9][10][11][12]:

  • Social Security, Veterans benefits, IRS final tax return, and Probate in the United States: Contact the Social Security Administration (phone: +1 800 772 1213; TTY: +1 800 325 0778) to report the death, stop ongoing monthly benefits, and claim the $255 lump-sum death payment and monthly survivor benefits (moreover, under the U.S.-Canada Social Security Totalization Agreement, work credits earned in both countries can be combined to meet eligibility thresholds) [9]. If the deceased was a U.S. military veteran, eligible survivors can apply to the Department of Veterans Affairs (phone: +1 800 827 1000) using VA Form 21P-530EZ for burial allowances, a headstone or marker, and national cemetery interment [10]. The executor or personal representative must also file a final federal income tax return (Form 1040, plus Form 1310 if claiming a refund) with the Internal Revenue Service (phone: +1 800 829 1040) and open probate proceedings in the county Probate Court of the deceased's U.S. state of domicile [11].
  • Canadian pensions (CPP/QPP), CRA tax clearance, and provincial estate administration in Canada: If the deceased resided, worked, or held property in Canada, notify Service Canada (phone: +1 800 622 6232; outside Canada/US: +1 613 957 1954) to cancel Old Age Security (OAS) and Social Insurance Number records and to apply for the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) Death Benefit (a one-time lump-sum payment to the estate) and monthly CPP Survivor's Pension (or contact Retraite Québec if the deceased contributed to the Québec Pension Plan - QPP) [9]. Finally, the legal representative of any Canadian estate or Canadian-source income must file a Final T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return with the Canada Revenue Agency (phone: +1 800 959 8281; from outside Canada/US: +1 613 940 8495) and apply for a CRA Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) [13] before distributing Canadian estate assets, alongside applying for a provincial Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee (probate) where Canadian banks or land registries require it [1][12].

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in United States: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in United States: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in United States, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and United States.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. When a citizen or resident of Canada dies in the United States, medical certification and civil death registration must first be completed in the U.S. state and county where the death occurred before remains or cremated ashes can be cleared through the Canada Border Services Agency and before survivor benefits, taxes, and probate are settled in Canada and the United States [1][4][7].

steps.title: Obtain Medical Certification of Death and Complete Any County Coroner or Medical Examiner Clearance in the United States
steps.html:
Before a funeral home in the United States can transfer the body across state or international borders or proceed with cremation, an authorized physician or county forensic official must certify the cause and manner of death [1][4].

  • Death in a hospital, hospice, or care facility: When a death occurs in a hospital or under hospice care from natural causes, the attending physician completes the medical certification in the state's electronic death registration system and authorizes the release of the body to the appointed funeral director [1]. Provide the deceased person's Canadian passport or provincial identity documents immediately so that their exact legal name, date and place of birth, and Canadian citizenship are recorded without error [4].
  • Sudden, accidental, or unattended death outside a hospital: If the death occurs unexpectedly at a private residence, seasonal accommodation, hotel, or public location, call 911 immediately. Local police and the county Coroner or Medical Examiner (for example, the District Medical Examiner in Florida, the Maricopa County Office of the Medical Examiner in Arizona, or the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner in California) must investigate, perform an autopsy if legally required, and issue forensic clearance before the body can be released for embalming, cremation, or repatriation [1][4].

steps.title: Check Travel Insurance, Appoint Licensed Funeral Directors in the United States and Canada, and Contact Canadian Consular Officials
steps.html:
Before entering into an independent funeral contract, check whether your family member carried Canadian travel medical insurance (such as a seasonal snowbird policy), credit-card travel protection, or employer group insurance [4]. Travel insurers normally require immediate notification to their 24/7 assistance center to authorize and fund repatriation or local cremation [4].

  • Appointing a licensed U.S. funeral director and FTC Funeral Rule protections: Locate a state-licensed funeral home in the U.S. county of death through the directory of the National Funeral Directors Association (phone: +1 262 789 1880; email: nfda@nfda.org) [2]. Clarvia provides directory information for orientation only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific funeral providers. Under the federal Funeral Rule enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (phone: +1 877 382 4357), every U.S. funeral provider must supply an itemized General Price List (GPL) at the start of arrangements, let you choose only the specific services required (such as direct cremation or international preparation and shipment), and explain any legal embalming requirements truthfully [3].
  • Coordinating with a receiving funeral provider in Canada and Canadian consular assistance: For full-body repatriation to Canada, the U.S. funeral director coordinates directly with a provincially licensed receiving funeral establishment in the destination Canadian province, such as a provider licensed by the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (phone: +1 844 493 6356 or +1 647 483 2649; email: info@thebao.ca), Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or provincial associations affiliated with the Funeral Service Association of Canada [5][6]. You can also contact the nearest Consulate General or Embassy of Canada in the United States or the 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre of Global Affairs Canada (phone from the US/Canada: +1 800 387 3124 or +1 613 996 8885; email: sos@international.gc.ca) for consular guidance and local provider lists [4].

steps.title: Register the Death with U.S. State Vital Records and Complete Document Recognition for Canada
steps.html:
The U.S. funeral director files the completed death registration with the county health department or state Vital Records office, which can be looked up for every U.S. state and territory via the National Center for Health Statistics (phone: +1 800 232 4636) Where to Write for Vital Records directory [1].

  • Ordering certified U.S. Death Certificates (including cause of death): Request multiple official certified copies of the U.S. state Death Certificate through the funeral director or state Vital Records office [1][4]. Ensure you obtain both certified copies that include the medical cause of death (required by the Canada Border Services Agency for importing uncremated remains and by life and travel insurers) and standard certified copies for banks, pensions, and probate courts (note that if the deceased held dual U.S.-Canadian citizenship and died outside the United States, a Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad, CRDA Form DS-2060, is issued by the U.S. Embassy or Consulate) [1][4][7].
  • Recognition of U.S. Death Certificates in Canada and Apostille rules: Provincial registries in Canada (such as ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) do not issue a provincial death certificate for a death that occurred outside their province (except where specific provincial provisions apply, such as inserting an act of death in the Quebec civil register for a domiciled resident) [4][5]. Instead, Canadian banks, courts, and government agencies accept the certified U.S. state Death Certificate (accompanied by a certified English or French translation if not in English) [4][5]. Because both the United States and Canada are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, if a Canadian probate court or land registry requires formal authentication of the U.S. Death Certificate, obtain an Apostille from the Secretary of State of the U.S. state where the death certificate was issued [4].

steps.title: Choose Between International Repatriation of Remains or Ashes to Canada and Local Burial or Cremation in the United States
steps.html:
Your U.S. and Canadian funeral directors handle the cross-border public-health, customs, and transit documentation depending on whether you choose full-body repatriation, ash transport, or local disposition [7][8]:

  • Repatriation of uncremated human remains from the United States to Canada: The U.S. funeral director obtains the state burial-transit permit (permit for disposition of human remains) and prepares the body for air cargo or land-border transport in accordance with U.S. state law, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (phone: +1 800 232 4636) human remains rules (42 CFR 71.55), and U.S. Customs and Border Protection export procedures [8]. For entry into Canada, Memorandum D19-9-3 of the Canada Border Services Agency (phone: +1 800 461 9999; outside Canada: +1 204 983 3500) and the Canadian Quarantine Act require the shipment to be accompanied by a certified copy of the U.S. Death Certificate stating the cause of death (or a coroner's/physician's statement confirming whether the deceased had a communicable disease of concern) and transported in a leak-proof or hermetically sealed container [4][7].
  • Transporting cremated ashes to Canada or local burial in the United States: Under Canada Border Services Agency Memorandum D19-9-3, cremated human remains do not pose a quarantine risk and are exempt from Quarantine Act communicable-disease restrictions [7]. A family member may transport cremated ashes into Canada by car or in airline carry-on luggage in a non-metallic, X-ray-scannable urn, declaring the ashes to the CBSA border officer with a copy of the U.S. Death Certificate and the Certificate of Cremation [4][7][8]. If the family chooses local burial or cremation in the United States, the U.S. funeral director secures the local county disposition/cremation permit directly [1][3].

steps.title: Complete Survivor Pension, Benefit, Tax, and Probate Steps in Canada and the United States
steps.html:
Once you have the certified U.S. Death Certificates, complete the post-death benefit claims, tax filings, and estate administration in both Canada and the United States [9][10][11][12]:

  • Canadian pensions (CPP/QPP, OAS), provincial health card cancellation, CRA taxes, and Probate: Notify Service Canada (phone: +1 800 622 6232; outside Canada/US: +1 613 957 1954) to cancel Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) retirement payments (any payment issued after the month of death must be returned) and to apply for the one-time lump-sum CPP Death Benefit and monthly CPP Survivor's Pension and children's benefits (or contact Retraite Québec if the deceased contributed to the Québec Pension Plan - QPP) [4][9]. Cancel the deceased's provincial health card, driver's licence, and passport (for example, through ServiceOntario at +1 800 461 2156 in Ontario) [4][5]. For Canadian tax and estate administration, the executor or estate trustee must file the deceased's Final T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return with the Canada Revenue Agency (phone: +1 800 959 8281; outside Canada/US: +1 613 940 8495), apply for a provincial grant of probate (such as a Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee in Ontario) where required by financial institutions or land registries, and request a CRA Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) before making final estate distributions [5][10].
  • U.S. Social Security, Veterans benefits, IRS tax filings, and U.S. Probate: If the deceased worked in the United States or received U.S. benefits, notify the Social Security Administration (phone: +1 800 772 1213; TTY: +1 800 325 0778) to report the death and check eligibility for survivor benefits or the $255 lump-sum death payment (noting that under the Canada-U.S. Social Security Agreement, periods of contribution in both countries can be coordinated) [9][11]. If the deceased served in the U.S. military, contact the Department of Veterans Affairs (phone: +1 800 827 1000) regarding burial allowances (VA Form 21P-530EZ) and memorial benefits [13]. Finally, if the deceased had U.S.-source income, U.S. tax residency, or U.S. real property (such as a vacation home in Florida or Arizona), file the required final federal tax return (Form 1040 or Form 1040-NR, and Form 706-NA if U.S.-situs assets exceed federal estate-tax filing thresholds) with the Internal Revenue Service (phone: +1 800 829 1040) and consult the county Probate Court in the U.S. state where any sole-name real property is located regarding ancillary probate [12].

cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of United States dies in United Kingdom: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in United Kingdom, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in United States and United Kingdom.
introHtml: We are sorry for your loss. When a citizen or resident of the United States dies in the United Kingdom, procedures depend on the UK constituent nation where the death occurred (England and Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland) and on the U.S. state of final disposition or residence. The five steps below set out the official sequence and who handles each action.

steps.title: Medical certification of death and coroner or procurator fiscal clearance in the United Kingdom
steps.html:
• Death in a hospital or care setting: In England and Wales, an attending doctor prepares the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD), which must be independently scrutinised and countersigned by an NHS Medical Examiner before being sent electronically to the local Register Office (for example, Westminster Register Office in London or Manchester Register Office) [1]. In Scotland, the certifying doctor issues Form 11 (Certificate of Registration of Death), subject to random review by the Healthcare Improvement Scotland Death Certification Review Service (DCRS) [1].
  • Death at a private address, hotel, or public place: Call emergency services on 999 (or NHS 111 if a doctor was already treating a terminal illness) so a medical practitioner and, where necessary, the police can attend and confirm the death [1].
  • Sudden, unexplained, or unnatural deaths: In England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the death is referred to the local Coroner, who must investigate the cause of death and issue clearance (or an interim certificate after a post-mortem) before registration or international transport can proceed [1]. In Scotland, unexpected deaths are reported to the Procurator Fiscal within the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service.

steps.title: Repatriation insurance, funeral directors in the United Kingdom and the United States, and U.S. consular assistance
steps.html:
• Check travel or repatriation insurance first: Before signing an independent funeral contract, check whether your family member held travel, medical-assistance, or employer coverage that includes international repatriation. If a policy applies, contact the insurer's 24-hour assistance desk immediately, as the insurer normally appoints the funeral coordinator and manages logistics directly [4].
  • Appointing a UK funeral director: If no insurer is managing the case, appoint an experienced UK funeral director through a recognised UK trade association such as the National Society of Allied and Independent Funeral Directors (or the National Association of Funeral Directors - NAFD) [4]. The UK provider coordinates mortuary care, UK export permits, and air cargo booking.
  • Appointing a receiving U.S. funeral home: If returning remains to the United States, select a licensed receiving funeral home in the destination U.S. state using the directory of the National Funeral Directors Association [5]. Under the Federal Trade Commission Funeral Rule, U.S. funeral providers must supply an itemised General Price List over the telephone and in person so you can choose only the services required to receive and inter or cremate the remains [6].
  • U.S. consular notification: Report the death to the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in the United Kingdom (in London, Edinburgh, or Belfast) via their online U.S. Citizen Services Navigator or emergency telephone line (+44 20 7499 9000) [2][3]. Consular officers guide next of kin on disposition options, safeguard personal effects if no relative is present, and prepare the U.S. consular death report, though the U.S. government cannot fund funeral or shipping costs [2][3].

steps.title: Civil death registration in the United Kingdom, apostille legalisation, and the U.S. Consular Report of Death Abroad
steps.html:
• Civil registration in the UK: Once the Medical Examiner (in England and Wales) or doctor (in Scotland) transmits the medical certificate, register the death at the local Register Office within 5 days in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, or within 8 days at any registration office in Scotland [1]. Request multiple certified copies of the full UK Death Certificate (standard fee GBP 12.50 per copy in England and Wales) and ask the registrar for your unique reference number for the Tell Us Once service [1][9].
  • Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad (CRDA): Submit a scanned copy of the UK death certificate and the deceased's U.S. passport to the U.S. Embassy and Consulates in the United Kingdom so they can issue the electronic Consular Report of Death of a U.S. Citizen Abroad (Form DS-2060) [2][3]. The CRDA serves as the primary English-language death record accepted by U.S. courts, banks, insurers, and federal agencies [2].
  • Apostille legalisation: Because UK certificates are already in English, translation is not needed for the United States, and neither the UK nor the US uses the multilingual CIEC Form C. If a U.S. state probate court, land registry, or financial institution requires formal authentication of the underlying UK Death Certificate in addition to the CRDA, your funeral director or solicitor can obtain a Hague Apostille from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office Legalisation Office [7].

steps.title: Repatriation of remains or ashes to the United States versus local burial or cremation in the United Kingdom
steps.html:
• Repatriation of non-cremated human remains: To move a body outside England or Wales, your UK funeral director applies to the local Coroner for an Out-of-England Order (Form 104) at least 4 clear days before departure; in Scotland, advance clearance is required from the Death Certification Review Service [1][4]. The body is embalmed and sealed in a leak-proof inner container inside an international shipping casket [8]. For entry into the United States under regulations of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (42 CFR 71.55), non-cremated remains consigned to a licensed U.S. mortuary or cemetery must be in a leak-proof container and accompanied by the official death certificate (or importer certification statement confirming no quarantinable communicable disease applies) [8]. U.S. Customs and Border Protection clears the shipment at the U.S. port of entry, where the receiving funeral home obtains the local state burial-transit permit.
  • Transporting cremated ashes: If cremation takes place in the UK first, cremated remains are exempt from CDC import permits under 42 CFR 71.55 [8]. They may be carried as hand luggage in a security-scannable (non-metallic) urn accompanied by the official UK death certificate and certificate of cremation, subject to airline rules and U.S. Customs and Border Protection inspection [3][8].
  • Local burial or cremation in the UK: If the family chooses burial or cremation in the UK without repatriation, the Register Office issues the Certificate for Burial or Cremation (the Green Form in England and Wales, or Form 14 in Scotland) directly to the UK funeral director once registration is complete [1].

steps.title: Post-death notifications, survivor benefits, tax filings, and probate in the United States and the United Kingdom
steps.html:
• United Kingdom notifications, pensions, and probate: Use the Tell Us Once reference number within 28 days of receiving it to notify HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), and local councils in one step [9]. If your family member had UK National Insurance contributions or a UK State Pension, contact the DWP Bereavement Service (or the International Pension Centre if living abroad) regarding Bereavement Support Payment or survivor entitlements [9]. If the deceased held UK real property or substantial UK bank accounts, the executor or administrator may need to report the estate value to HMRC and apply for a Grant of Probate (or Letters of Administration) through HM Courts and Tribunals Service in England and Wales, or Confirmation through the Sheriff Court in Scotland [10].
  • United States Social Security and Veterans benefits: Report the death to the Social Security Administration by calling 1-800-772-1213 (from within the U.S.) or by contacting the Federal Benefits Unit at the U.S. Embassy in London (+44 20 7499 9000) if residing in the UK [3][11]. Eligible surviving relatives may claim the one-time USD 255 lump-sum death payment and monthly survivor benefits, and any Social Security payment received for the month of death must be returned [11]. If the deceased served in the U.S. armed forces, contact the Department of Veterans Affairs regarding burial allowances (VA Form 21P-530EZ), national cemetery interment, or memorial items [12].
  • United States tax filings and state probate: The personal representative or surviving relative must file a final federal income tax return (Form 1040, marked "DECEASED" with the date of death) with the Internal Revenue Service covering income from January 1 through the date of death, due by the regular April filing deadline of the following year (and Form 1041 if the estate generates post-death income) [13]. For U.S. real estate or financial accounts that do not pass automatically by beneficiary designation or joint ownership, petition the local county Probate Court (or Surrogate's Court) in the U.S. state where your family member was domiciled or owned property, submitting the CRDA and original will.

closingQuestion: To help tailor this further: 1. In which UK nation and municipality did the death occur, and in which U.S. state was your family member domiciled or will final arrangements take place? 2. Are you planning international repatriation of the body, cremation in the UK followed by transporting the ashes to the United States, or local burial/cremation in the UK?
