title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in Mexico: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in Mexico: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in Mexico: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in Mexico, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and Mexico.
introHtml: We extend our sincere condolences on the death in Mexico of your family member with citizenship or residence ties to Canada. Below is the chronological five-step official guide integrating the medical, sanitary, civil registration, consular, and estate procedures applicable in both Mexico and Canada.

steps.title: Medical Certification of Death and Forensic Clearance in Mexico
steps.html:
The first mandatory document in Mexico is the medical death certificate (Certificado de Defunción), regulated by the Secretaría de Salud (Ministry of Health), which certifies the medical cause of death and is indispensable for civil registration, sanitary permits, and any repatriation procedure [1][2].

  • Death in a hospital or clinic: If the death occurs in a public or private medical facility in Mexico, the licensed attending physician issues the Certificado de Defunción directly and free of charge after verifying the deceased person's identity (using their Canadian passport or immigration document) [1].
  • Death at home, in a hotel, or in a public place: If the deceased was receiving ongoing medical care in Mexico for a diagnosed chronic illness and dies of natural causes at a private residence, the attending physician may attend and certify the death [1]. However, if the death occurs suddenly or without prior medical attendance, in a hotel, tourist accommodation, or public place, or from accidental causes or circumstances subject to investigation, the body must not be moved: call the national emergency number 911 immediately [1][4]. In these cases, the Public Prosecutor (Ministerio Público) of the state Attorney General's Office (Fiscalía General de Justicia) intervenes and transfers the body to the Forensic Medical Service (Servicio Médico Forense - SEMEFO) for a statutory autopsy before issuing the Certificado de Defunción and authorizing release of the remains [1][4].
  • 12-to-48-hour sanitary timeframe: Under the General Health Law Regulation on Sanitary Control of the Disposition of Human Organs, Tissues, and Cadavers overseen by the Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios (COFEPRIS, Federal Commission for the Protection against Sanitary Risk), burial, cremation, or sanitary preparation (embalming or authorized refrigeration) must generally take place between 12 and 48 hours after death, unless otherwise ordered by the Ministerio Público or the health authority [2].

steps.title: Travel or Repatriation Insurance, Licensed Funeral Directors, and Canadian Consular Assistance
steps.html:
Because sanitary timeframes in Mexico are short, you should immediately check insurance coverage, appoint licensed funeral providers in both countries, and notify Canadian consular authorities.

  • Checking travel or repatriation insurance: Verify whether the deceased held a Canadian travel medical insurance policy, credit card coverage, or employer insurance including a funeral assistance and repatriation clause [4]. If an active policy exists, contact the insurer's 24-hour assistance center before signing private funeral contracts, as insurers usually appoint and directly pay the funeral providers handling international repatriation [4].
  • Licensed funeral agency in Mexico and receiving funeral home in Canada: In Mexico, engage a legally established funeral agency (agencia funeraria) holding an operating notice and sanitary license with the Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios or state health authority (COEPRIS) and a standard consumer contract registered with the Federal Consumer Protection Agency (Procuraduría Federal del Consumidor - PROFECO) [2]. If repatriating the body to Canada, the Mexican funeral home coordinates with a provincially licensed receiving funeral provider in the destination Canadian province or territory (for example, a provider licensed by the Bereavement Authority of Ontario in Ontario, Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or affiliated with the Funeral Service Association of Canada) [4][5]. Clarvia provides references to regulatory bodies and professional associations for informational guidance only and does not endorse, recommend, or rank individual commercial providers.
  • Notifying Canadian consular authorities: Contact the Embajada de Canadá en México (Embassy of Canada to Mexico in Mexico City, phone +52 55 5724 7900, email mex@international.gc.ca, or the Canadian consulates and consular agencies in Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Vallarta, Guadalajara, Cabo San Lucas, Mazatlán, Monterrey, or Tijuana) or the 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre of Global Affairs Canada in Ottawa (+1 613 996 8885, email sos@international.gc.ca) [3][4]. Consular officers guide the family on local procedures, help verify local service providers, coordinate official communication with Mexican authorities, and administratively cancel the deceased person's Canadian passport [3][4].

steps.title: Civil Registration in Mexico, Apostille, and Document Recognition in Canada
steps.html:
With the original Certificado de Defunción issued by the physician or SEMEFO, the family or authorized funeral agency must register the death with the Mexican civil registry [1].

  • Civil Death Certificate (Acta de Defunción) and permits in Mexico: Appear before the local Civil Registry Office (Oficialía or Juzgado del Registro Civil) of the municipality or borough where the death occurred, presenting the Certificado de Defunción and the deceased person's passport [1][2]. The Civil Registry records the death and issues the official Acta de Defunción (civil death certificate) along with the official burial, cremation, or transit permit (permiso de inhumación, cremación o traslado) [1][2]. Request several certified copies of the Acta de Defunción for both Mexican exit formalities and banking, tax, and estate administration in Canada [1][4].
  • Hague Apostille and certified translation for Canada: Neither Mexico nor Canada is a party to CIEC Convention No. 16 (multilingual Form C), but both countries are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention (in force for Canada since January 2024). For the Mexican Acta de Defunción to have full legal validity before authorities and institutions in Canada, it must receive an Apostille from the Secretaría de Gobierno of the Mexican state where it was issued (or from the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores for federal documents) and be accompanied by a certified translation into English or French [1][4].
  • Provincial Vital Statistics registries in Canada: Provincial and territorial Vital Statistics offices in Canada (such as ServiceOntario in Ontario or BC Vital Statistics in British Columbia) generally do not register deaths that occur outside their province; instead, the apostilled and translated Mexican Acta de Defunción is used directly with Canadian banks, probate courts, and federal agencies [4][6]. As an important exception, if the deceased was domiciled in Quebec, the Directeur de l'état civil of Quebec allows families to apply for insertion (insertion d'un acte fait hors du Québec) of the foreign death record into the Quebec civil status register [4].

steps.title: International Repatriation of Remains or Ashes to Canada vs. Local Burial or Cremation in Mexico
steps.html:
The family must choose between transporting the body or cremated ashes to Canada or arranging final disposition in Mexico, complying with the health and customs regulations of both countries.

  • Repatriating the body in a casket to Canada: Exporting remains from Mexico requires the Acta de Defunción, the official certificate of embalming or sanitary preparation, the international mortuary transit permit (permiso sanitario de traslado internacional de cadáveres) issued by the Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios or state health services, and placement in a hermetically sealed casket with a sealed metal inner liner meeting public health and IATA air transport standards [2][4]. Upon arrival in Canada, the Canada Border Services Agency enforces the Quarantine Act in accordance with Memorandum D19-9-3 [5]: the shipment must be accompanied by the official death certificate stating the cause of death (to verify whether the person had a listed communicable disease subject to quarantine), the transit permit, and the embalming or hermetic-sealing certificate, with a translation into English or French [5].
  • Repatriating cremated ashes to Canada: If cremation takes place in Mexico with authorization from the Civil Registry (and from the Ministerio Público whenever SEMEFO was involved), transporting the ashes to Canada is considerably simpler [2][5]. Under Memorandum D19-9-3 of the Canada Border Services Agency, cremated human remains do not pose a quarantine risk under the Quarantine Act and may enter Canada in carry-on baggage or as air cargo accompanied by a copy of the Acta de Defunción and the official cremation certificate, in an X-ray scan-friendly urn free of prohibited materials [5].
  • Local burial or cremation in Mexico: If you choose burial or cremation in the Mexican municipality where the death occurred, the licensed funeral agency obtains the local permit directly from the Civil Registry and municipal health authority within the statutory 12-to-48-hour timeframe [1][2].

steps.title: Survivor Pensions, Funeral Benefits, Taxes, and Probate in Canada and Mexico
steps.html:
Once you have obtained certified, apostilled, and translated copies of the Acta de Defunción, complete the social security, tax, and estate steps in both jurisdictions.

  • Benefits and pensions in Canada (Service Canada and Retraite Québec): Notify Service Canada of the death to cancel Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) payments and prevent overpayments [6]. Through Service Canada, the estate or the person who paid the funeral expenses can apply for the CPP Death Benefit (a one-time lump-sum payment of up to CAD 2,500), and eligible survivors can claim the CPP Survivor's Pension and children's benefits using Forms ISP1200 and ISP1300 [6]. If the deceased contributed in the province of Quebec, these benefits (prestation de décès and rente de conjoint survivant) are claimed from Retraite Québec under the Quebec Pension Plan (QPP/RRQ) [6].
  • Tax obligations and Probate in Canada: The legal representative or executor (liquidateur in Quebec) must notify the Canada Revenue Agency, file the deceased's Final T1 Return, and - before distributing Canadian estate assets - apply for a tax Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) from the Canada Revenue Agency [7]. Will probate or estate administration (Grant of Probate, Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee in Ontario, or notarial/judicial verification in Quebec) is filed with the superior or probate court of the Canadian province where the deceased was domiciled or held property [4][7].
  • Social security benefits and AFORE pension withdrawal in Mexico: If the deceased resided or worked in Mexico and contributed to the Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (IMSS, phone 800 623 23 23), the person who paid the funeral bill in Mexico may claim the funeral expense grant (ayuda para gastos de funeral, equal to twice the monthly UMA value) within one year, and eligible dependents may apply for a widow's or orphan's pension [8]. If the deceased was a Mexican public-sector employee or pensioner affiliated with the Instituto de Seguridad y Servicios Sociales de los Trabajadores del Estado (ISSSTE), beneficiaries may claim the 120-day funeral grant (pago de marcha) and survivor pensions [9]. Additionally, if the deceased held an individual retirement savings account in Mexico, beneficiaries may apply to the relevant AFORE, regulated by the Comisión Nacional del Sistema de Ahorro para el Retiro (CONSAR), to withdraw accumulated pension funds [10].
  • Estate succession and tax deregistration in Mexico: If the deceased left real estate or bank accounts in Mexico, consult a Mexican civil-law notary (notario público affiliated with the Colegio Nacional del Notariado Mexicano) or family court judge in Mexico to request an official search of the National Register of Will Notices (Registro Nacional de Avisos de Testamento - RENAT), coordinated by the Secretaría de Gobernación (Ministry of the Interior), and conduct testamentary or intestate succession in Mexico [11]. Finally, if the deceased was registered in the Mexican Federal Taxpayer Registry (RFC), file the notice of RFC cancellation due to death (aviso de cancelación en el RFC por defunción, procedure sheet 83/CFF) with the Mexican Tax Administration Service (Servicio de Administración Tributaria - SAT) within one month following the death [12].

closingQuestion: To provide guidance tailored to your situation, in which municipality and state of Mexico did the death occur, to which Canadian province and city do you plan to transport the remains or handle estate administration, and do you prefer to repatriate the body or cremated ashes or arrange local disposition in Mexico?

es.title: Qué hacer ante un fallecimiento entre México y Canadá: lista oficial en 5 pasos
es.cardSummary: Guía oficial en 5 pasos tras un fallecimiento entre México y Canadá: certificado médico de defunción, funeraria autorizada, inscripción en el Registro Civil, trámites consulares y repatriación o entierro local, y pensiones de supervivencia y sucesión.
es.introHtml: Lamentamos el fallecimiento de su familiar con vínculos de ciudadanía o residencia en Canadá ocurrido en México. A continuación se presenta la guía oficial en cinco pasos ordenada cronológicamente, integrando los procedimientos médicos, sanitarios, registrales, consulares y sucesorios aplicables tanto en México como en Canadá.

steps.title: Certificación médica de la defunción y liberación forense en México
steps.html:
El primer documento obligatorio en territorio mexicano es el Certificado de Defunción, regulado por la Secretaría de Salud, el cual acredita las causas médicas del fallecimiento y resulta indispensable para el registro civil, los permisos sanitarios y cualquier trámite de repatriación [1][2].

  • Fallecimiento en hospital o clínica: Si el deceso ocurre en una unidad médica pública o privada en México, el médico tratante con cédula profesional expide directamente y sin costo el Certificado de Defunción tras verificar la identidad de la persona fallecida (mediante su pasaporte canadiense o documento migratorio) [1].
  • Fallecimiento en domicilio, hotel o vía pública: Si la persona fallecida recibía atención médica en México por una enfermedad crónica diagnosticada y muere por causas naturales en un domicilio particular, el médico tratante puede acudir a certificar la defunción [1]. En cambio, si el fallecimiento ocurre de forma súbita o sin asistencia médica previa, en un hotel, alojamiento turístico o en la vía pública, o por causas accidentales o sujetas a investigación, no se debe mover el cuerpo: llame de inmediato al número nacional de emergencias 911 [1][4]. En estos casos interviene el Ministerio Público de la Fiscalía General de Justicia de la entidad federativa correspondiente y el cuerpo es trasladado al Servicio Médico Forense (SEMEFO) para practicar la necropsia de ley antes de emitir el Certificado de Defunción y autorizar la entrega de los restos [1][4].
  • Plazo sanitario de 12 a 48 horas: Conforme al Reglamento de la Ley General de Salud en Materia de Control Sanitario de la Disposición de Órganos, Tejidos y Cadáveres de Seres Humanos vigilado por la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios, la inhumación, cremación o preparación sanitaria (embalsamamiento o refrigeración autorizada) debe realizarse por regla general entre las 12 y las 48 horas posteriores al deceso, salvo disposición específica del Ministerio Público o de la autoridad sanitaria [2].

steps.title: Seguro de viaje o repatriación, agencias funerarias autorizadas y asistencia consular de Canadá
steps.html:
Dado que los plazos sanitarios en México son breves, conviene activar de inmediato la cobertura aseguradora, designar proveedores funerarios autorizados en ambos países y dar aviso consular.

  • Verificación de seguro de viaje o repatriación: Revise si la persona fallecida contaba con una póliza canadiense de seguro médico de viaje, cobertura de tarjeta de crédito o seguro laboral con cláusula de asistencia y repatriación funeraria [4]. Si existe póliza vigente, comuníquese con la central de asistencia de la aseguradora antes de firmar contratos particulares, ya que las compañías suelen designar y cubrir directamente a las agencias funerarias encargadas del traslado internacional [4].
  • Agencia funeraria en México y funeraria receptora en Canadá: En México, contrate una agencia funeraria legalmente establecida que cuente con aviso de funcionamiento y licencia sanitaria ante la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios o la autoridad sanitaria estatal (COEPRIS) y con contrato de adhesión registrado ante la Procuraduría Federal del Consumidor (PROFECO) [2]. Si se opta por repatriar el cuerpo a Canadá, la funeraria mexicana debe coordinarse con un proveedor funerario con licencia provincial en la provincia o territorio canadiense de destino (por ejemplo, un establecimiento regulado por la Bereavement Authority of Ontario en Ontario, Consumer Protection BC en Columbia Británica, o afiliado a la Funeral Service Association of Canada) [4][5]. Clarvia facilita referencias a organismos reguladores y asociaciones profesionales únicamente a título orientativo y no respalda, recomienda ni clasifica a proveedores comerciales individuales.
  • Notificación a las autoridades consulares canadienses: Comuníquese con la Embajada de Canadá en México (ubicada en Ciudad de México, teléfono +52 55 5724 7900, correo electrónico mex@international.gc.ca, o con las agencias y consulados en Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Vallarta, Guadalajara, Cabo San Lucas, Mazatlán, Monterrey o Tijuana) o bien con el Centro de Vigilancia y Respuesta de Emergencia las 24 horas de Global Affairs Canada en Ottawa (+1 613 996 8885, correo sos@international.gc.ca) [3][4]. El personal consular orienta a la familia sobre los procedimientos locales, ayuda a verificar proveedores locales, coordina la comunicación oficial con autoridades mexicanas y procede a la cancelación administrativa del pasaporte canadiense de la persona fallecida [3][4].

steps.title: Inscripción en el Registro Civil en México, apostilla y reconocimiento de documentos en Canadá
steps.html:
Con el Certificado de Defunción original expedido por el médico o el SEMEFO, la familia o la agencia funeraria autorizada debe inscribir el fallecimiento ante la autoridad civil mexicana [1].

  • Acta de Defunción y permisos en México: Acuda a la Oficialía o Juzgado del Registro Civil del municipio o alcaldía donde ocurrió el deceso presentando el Certificado de Defunción y el pasaporte de la persona fallecida [1][2]. El Registro Civil levanta el registro oficial y expide el Acta de Defunción junto con la boleta o permiso oficial de inhumación, cremación o traslado [1][2]. Solicite varias copias certificadas del Acta de Defunción tanto para los trámites de salida de México como para las gestiones bancarias, fiscales y sucesorias en Canadá [1][4].
  • Apostilla de La Haya y traducción oficial para Canadá: Ni México ni Canadá forman parte del Convenio n.º 16 de la CIEC (Formulario C plurilingüe), pero ambos países son partes del Convenio de La Haya de 1961 sobre la Apostilla (en vigor para Canadá desde enero de 2024). Para que el Acta de Defunción mexicana tenga plena validez jurídica ante las autoridades e instituciones de Canadá, debe apostillarse ante la Secretaría de Gobierno de la entidad federativa mexicana donde fue emitida (o ante la Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores en el caso de documentos federales) y acompañarse de una traducción certificada al inglés o al francés [1][4].
  • Registros provinciales en Canadá (Vital Statistics): Los registros civiles provinciales o territoriales de Canadá (como ServiceOntario en Ontario o BC Vital Statistics en Columbia Británica) por regla general no inscriben defunciones ocurridas fuera de su provincia; en su lugar, el Acta de Defunción mexicana debidamente apostillada y traducida se utiliza directamente ante bancos, tribunales de sucesión y organismos federales canadienses [4][6]. Como excepción relevante, si la persona fallecida estaba domiciliada en Quebec, el Directeur de l'état civil de Québec permite solicitar la inserción (inscripción) del acta de defunción extranjera en el registro del estado civil de Quebec [4].

steps.title: Repatriación internacional de restos o cenizas a Canadá frente a inhumación o cremación local en México
steps.html:
La familia debe elegir entre trasladar el cuerpo o las cenizas a Canadá o realizar la disposición final en territorio mexicano, cumpliendo las normas sanitarias y aduaneras de ambos países.

  • Repatriación del cuerpo en féretro a Canadá: Para la salida de México se requiere el Acta de Defunción, el certificado oficial de embalsamamiento o preparación sanitaria, el permiso sanitario de traslado internacional de cadáveres expedido por la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios o los Servicios de Salud estatales, y el encierro en un féretro hermético con caja metálica interior sellada conforme a las normas sanitarias y de transporte aéreo IATA [2][4]. Para el ingreso a Canadá, la Canada Border Services Agency aplica las disposiciones de la Quarantine Act conforme al Memorándum D19-9-3 [5]: el envío debe ir acompañado del certificado o acta oficial de defunción que indique la causa de muerte (para verificar si existía una enfermedad transmisible sujeta a cuarentena), el permiso de traslado y el certificado de embalsamamiento o declaración de féretro hermético, con traducción al inglés o francés [5].
  • Repatriación de cenizas a Canadá: Si se realiza la cremación en México con autorización del Registro Civil (y del Ministerio Público cuando haya intervenido el SEMEFO), el traslado de las cenizas a Canadá es considerablemente más sencillo [2][5]. Conforme al Memorándum D19-9-3 de la Canada Border Services Agency, las cenizas humanas cremadas no constituyen un riesgo cuarentenario bajo la Quarantine Act y pueden ingresar a Canadá en equipaje de mano o como carga aérea acompañadas de una copia del Acta de Defunción y del certificado oficial de cremación en una urna libre de materiales prohibidos que permita el escaneo de rayos X [5].
  • Inhumación o cremación local en México: Si se opta por sepultar o cremar los restos en el municipio mexicano del fallecimiento, la agencia funeraria autorizada gestiona el permiso directamente ante el Registro Civil y la autoridad sanitaria local dentro del plazo legal de 12 a 48 horas [1][2].

steps.title: Pensiones de sobrevivencia, prestaciones funerarias, impuestos y sucesión en Canadá y en México
steps.html:
Una vez obtenidas las copias certificadas del Acta de Defunción (apostilladas y traducidas), gestione las notificaciones de seguridad social, impuestos y sucesión en ambas jurisdicciones.

  • Prestaciones y pensiones en Canadá (Service Canada y Retraite Québec): Notifique el fallecimiento a Service Canada para cancelar los pagos de Old Age Security (OAS) y del Canada Pension Plan (CPP) a fin de evitar cobros indebidos [6]. A través de Service Canada, el patrimonio o quien pagó el funeral puede solicitar el CPP Death Benefit (prestación única por fallecimiento de hasta 2 500 CAD), y los familiares con derecho pueden tramitar la CPP Survivor's Pension y prestaciones para hijos sobrevivientes mediante los formularios ISP1200 e ISP1300 [6]. Si la persona fallecida cotizó en la provincia de Quebec, estas prestaciones (prestation de décès y rente de conjoint survivant) se solicitan ante Retraite Québec bajo el Régime de rentes du Québec (QPP/RRQ) [6].
  • Obligaciones fiscales y sucesión (Probate) en Canadá: El representante legal o albacea (executor / liquidateur) debe notificar a la Canada Revenue Agency, presentar la declaración final de impuestos sobre la renta (Final T1 Return) y, antes de distribuir los bienes del caudal hereditario canadiense, solicitar el Certificado de Liquidación Fiscal (Clearance Certificate, Formulario TX19) ante la Canada Revenue Agency [7]. La validación del testamento o el nombramiento de administrador (Grant of Probate, Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee en Ontario, o verificación notarial/judicial en Quebec) se tramita ante el tribunal superior de la provincia donde la persona fallecida tenía su domicilio o bienes en Canadá [4][7].
  • Prestaciones de seguridad social y retiro de AFORE en México: Si la persona fallecida residía o trabajaba en México y cotizaba ante el Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social (teléfono 800 623 23 23), quien cubrió el funeral en México puede reclamar la ayuda para gastos de funeral (equivalente a dos veces el valor mensual de la UMA) dentro del plazo de un año y los beneficiarios legales pueden solicitar pensión de viudez u orfandad [8]. Si era persona trabajadora o pensionada del Estado afiliada al Instituto de Seguridad y Servicios Sociales de los Trabajadores del Estado, se puede gestionar el pago de marcha (120 días de pensión) y las pensiones por causa de muerte [9]. Asimismo, si tenía una cuenta individual de ahorro para el retiro, los beneficiarios pueden acudir a la AFORE correspondiente, regulada por la Comisión Nacional del Sistema de Ahorro para el Retiro, para retirar los recursos acumulados [10].
  • Sucesión patrimonial y baja fiscal en México: Si la persona fallecida dejó bienes inmuebles o cuentas bancarias en México, acuda ante un notario público (vinculado al Colegio Nacional del Notariado Mexicano) o juez familiar en México para que solicite el informe oficial al Registro Nacional de Avisos de Testamento, coordinado por la Secretaría de Gobernación, y tramite la sucesión testamentaria o intestamentaria mexicana [11]. Finalmente, si la persona fallecida estaba inscrita como contribuyente en México, presente el aviso de cancelación en el RFC por defunción (ficha 83/CFF) ante el Servicio de Administración Tributaria dentro del mes siguiente al deceso [12].

es.closingQuestion: Para ofrecerle indicaciones adaptadas a su situación, ¿en qué municipio y estado de México ocurrió el fallecimiento, hacia qué provincia y ciudad de Canadá se prevé el traslado o los trámites sucesorios, y desean realizar la repatriación del cuerpo o de las cenizas o bien la disposición local en México?

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in India: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in India: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in India: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in India, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and India.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. Managing cross-border arrangements between India and Canada involves coordinating medical and civil registration authorities in India with Canadian consular, border, and provincial or federal agencies. Below are the five official steps in order.

steps.title: Medical Certification of Death and Emergency or Forensic Clearance in India
steps.html:
Before civil registration, cremation, burial, or international transport can proceed, a cause of death must be formally certified in India [1][2].

  • Death in a hospital or medical facility: The attending physician issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Form 4) under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, and provides the hospital death summary required by the local registrar [2].
  • Death outside a hospital (residence, hotel, or public place): If your family member died at a private residence or hotel under natural circumstances, a registered medical practitioner who attended the person issues Form 4A [2].
  • Sudden, accidental, or unexplained death: Call India's national emergency number (112) immediately so the local police station can record a First Information Report (FIR) or inquest report (Panchnama) and transfer the deceased to a government hospital for a medico-legal post-mortem examination [1][2]. Keep the police No Objection Certificate (NOC) and post-mortem report, as both are required for funeral release and international transport.

steps.title: Insurance Notification, Funeral Coordination, and Consular Assistance
steps.html:
Before making independent financial commitments, check whether your family member held travel, medical-assistance, or employer repatriation insurance, as the insurer's assistance team often coordinates and funds the international transfer directly [1].

  • Consular notification and support: Contact the High Commission of Canada in India in New Delhi (or the Consulates General in Mumbai or Bengaluru, or Global Affairs Canada's 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre at +1 613-996-8885 or sos@international.gc.ca) [1][3]. Consular officers can provide lists of local funeral providers, explain local procedures, and cancel the deceased's Canadian passport [1][3].
  • Appointing funeral coordinators: You can mandate an authorized international funeral and human remains cargo provider in India (using the consular list or local municipal mortuary services) alongside a provincially licensed receiving funeral home in Canada [1][4]. In Canada, funeral providers are regulated at the provincial level, such as through the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (+1 647-496-4029, info@thebao.ca), Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or member directories of the Funeral Service Association of Canada [4]. These bodies and directories are provided as public-source examples for orientation; Clarvia does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific providers.

steps.title: Civil Death Registration in India and Document Legalization for Canada
steps.html:
Every death in India must be registered within 21 days with the local Registrar of Births and Deaths where the death occurred (such as the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation in Mumbai, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, or the local Gram Panchayat) through the Civil Registration System [2].

  • Obtaining official death certificates: When a death occurs in a hospital, the hospital typically transmits the medical notification directly to the local registrar so the family or appointed funeral coordinator can obtain multiple certified copies of the official Death Certificate from the Civil Registration System portal [2].
  • Apostille and recognition in Canada: Because both India and Canada are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, Indian death certificates used for estate, banking, or pension administration in Canada should receive an Apostille from the Ministry of External Affairs in India (following state-level pre-authentication by the State Home Department or Sub-Divisional Magistrate, or via the digital e-Sanad portal) [5]. If the certificate is not issued in English or French, obtain a certified translation [1]. Note that Canadian provincial Vital Statistics registries (such as ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) only register deaths occurring within their province; for deaths in India, the apostilled Indian Death Certificate serves as the primary legal proof of death in Canada [1].

steps.title: International Repatriation to Canada vs. Local Cremation or Burial in India
steps.html:
Your family can choose either to repatriate the body or cremated ashes to Canada or to hold a local funeral in India [1].

  • Repatriating human remains (casket) to Canada: Your appointed funeral coordinator in India arranges arterial embalming, hermetically sealed coffining in accordance with international air transport standards, a local police and municipal health NOC, and passport cancellation [1][6]. Under rules enforced by the Canada Border Services Agency on behalf of the Public Health Agency of Canada under the Quarantine Act (Memorandum D19-9-3), human remains entering Canada must be accompanied by an official Death Certificate stating the cause of death, proof that the deceased did not die of a Listed Communicable Disease (or meets hermetically sealed container rules), and an embalming/leak-proof casket certificate [7].
  • Transporting cremated ashes to Canada: If cremation takes place in India (at a municipal or community crematorium), the Canada Border Services Agency does not subject cremated human remains to Quarantine Act restrictions, provided the urn is accompanied by a certified copy of the death certificate and the official cremation certificate [7]. Check your airline's security screening rules for carry-on or cargo transport of the urn [1].
  • Note on Indian consular or health clearances: If the deceased held Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status or Indian nationality and any movement passes through Indian airport health authorities, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare operates the Airport Health Organization (APHO) and the eCARe portal for afterlife remains clearance [6].

steps.title: Post-Death Benefits, Pensions, Taxes, and Estate Administration in Canada and India
steps.html:
Once you have the official Indian Death Certificate (and its Apostille), you can complete pension, tax, and estate filings in both countries.

  • Pensions and federal benefits in Canada: Notify Service Canada (1-800-277-9914) to stop Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) retirement payments and to apply for the one-time CPP Death Benefit, the CPP Survivor's Pension, and children's benefits (or contact Retraite Québec if the person contributed to the Quebec Pension Plan) [8].
  • Tax filings and estate clearance in Canada: Notify the Canada Revenue Agency (1-800-959-8281) to report the date of death, file the deceased's Final T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return (and any T3 Trust Return for the estate), and enable the legal representative to request a Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) before distributing estate assets [9]. Provincial probate (such as a Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee in Ontario or a Grant of Probate in British Columbia) is filed with the relevant provincial superior or probate court if the deceased held sole-name Canadian real estate or financial accounts above institutional waiver thresholds.
  • Provident fund, insurance, and estate steps in India: If your family member held employment, bank accounts, or property in India, eligible nominees or legal heirs can submit the Composite Claim Form to the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (1800-118-005, employeefeedback@epfindia.gov.in) for Provident Fund withdrawal, Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance (EDLI), and Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) survivor pension [10], or claim benefits under the Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) or Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY) if applicable. For Indian bank accounts or real property without a registered nomination, families obtain a Legal Heir Certificate from the local Tehsildar/revenue office or a Succession Certificate / Probate from the competent Indian civil court.

Have you decided whether to arrange local cremation or burial in India or to repatriate the body or cremated ashes to Canada?

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in Philippines: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in Philippines: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in Philippines: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in Philippines, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and Philippines.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. Managing a death in the Philippines for a person with citizenship or residence ties to Canada involves coordinating local health, police, and civil registry steps in the Philippines with Canadian consular, border, and federal or provincial authorities. Below are the five official steps in order.

steps.title: Medical Certification of Death and Emergency or Forensic Clearance in the Philippines
steps.html:
Before local funeral arrangements, civil registration, or international transport can proceed, the cause of death must be formally certified in the Philippines [1][2].

  • Death in a hospital or medical facility: The attending physician completes the medical portion of the Certificate of Death (Municipal Form No. 103) and the hospital health officer reviews it before release to the licensed mortuary [2][3].
  • Death outside a hospital (residence, hotel, or public place): Report the death immediately to the local Barangay and the Philippine National Police (911) so authorities can verify whether the death was natural or requires a medico-legal investigation [1][2]. For natural deaths outside a hospital without an attending physician, the Municipal Health Officer (MHO) or City Health Officer (CHO) examines the deceased and certifies the cause of death on Municipal Form No. 103 [2].
  • 48-hour sanitation rule under Presidential Decree No. 856: Under Chapter XXI of the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines (PD 856), unembalmed human remains must generally be buried or cremated within 48 hours of death unless arterial embalming is performed by a licensed embalmer at an accredited mortuary [2].

steps.title: Insurance Notification, Funeral Coordination, and Consular Assistance
steps.html:
Before committing to private repatriation expenses, check whether your family member had travel, medical-assistance, or employer repatriation insurance, as the insurer's assistance service typically appoints the international funeral providers directly [1].

  • Consular notification and support: Contact the Embassy of Canada in the Philippines in Makati City, Metro Manila (or the Consulate of Canada in Cebu, or Global Affairs Canada's 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre at +1 613-996-8885 or sos@international.gc.ca) [1][4]. Canadian consular officers can provide a list of local funeral establishments experienced in international repatriation, liaise with Philippine authorities, and cancel the deceased's Canadian passport [1][4].
  • Appointing funeral coordinators: Mandate a funeral establishment and mortuary licensed by the Department of Health in the Philippines alongside a provincially licensed receiving funeral home in Canada [1][2][5]. In Canada, funeral providers are regulated at the provincial level, such as through the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (+1 647-496-4029, info@thebao.ca), Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or member directories of the Funeral Service Association of Canada [5]. These bodies and directories are listed as public-source examples for orientation; Clarvia does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific providers.

steps.title: Civil Death Registration in the Philippines and Document Legalization for Canada
steps.html:
Under Philippine civil registration law, the Certificate of Death (Municipal Form No. 103) must be registered within 30 days of death with the Local Civil Registrar's Office (LCRO) of the city or municipality where the death occurred (for example, the Manila Civil Registry Office, Quezon City Civil Registry Department, or Cebu City Civil Registrar) [3].

  • Obtaining official death certificates: After LCRO registration, request certified true copies from the LCRO for immediate transport permits and request the official Death Certificate printed on Security Paper (SECPA) from the Philippine Statistics Authority [3].
  • Apostille and recognition in Canada: Because both the Philippines and Canada are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention, the SECPA Death Certificate issued by the Philippine Statistics Authority should be authenticated with an Apostille from the Department of Foreign Affairs in the Philippines so it is recognized by Canadian banks, courts, and government agencies [1][6]. Provincial Vital Statistics registries in Canada (such as ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) only register deaths occurring within their province, so the apostilled Philippine Death Certificate serves as the official proof of death in Canada [1].

steps.title: International Repatriation to Canada vs. Local Burial or Cremation in the Philippines
steps.html:
Your family can choose either international repatriation of the body or cremated ashes to Canada or local burial or cremation in the Philippines [1].

  • Repatriating human remains (casket) from the Philippines to Canada: Your Philippine funeral director obtains the local burial/transfer permit from the City or Municipal Health Officer, completes full embalming and hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffining, and secures a Quarantine Permit for the international shipment of human remains from the Department of Health Bureau of Quarantine (BOQ) [2]. Upon arrival in Canada, the Canada Border Services Agency enforces Quarantine Act rules (Memorandum D19-9-3) requiring an official Death Certificate stating the cause of death, proof of freedom from Listed Communicable Diseases (or hermetically sealed containment), and an embalming/leak-proof casket certificate [7].
  • Transporting cremated ashes to Canada: If cremation takes place in the Philippines, obtain the official Cremation Certificate, certified Death Certificate, and BOQ quarantine clearance [2]. The Canada Border Services Agency does not impose Quarantine Act restrictions on cremated human remains entering Canada when accompanied by the death certificate and cremation certificate [7].
  • Dual nationals or Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs): If the deceased also held Philippine citizenship or OFW ties, check eligibility for repatriation and bereavement assistance through the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), or Philippine consular Report of Death procedures where applicable.

steps.title: Post-Death Benefits, Pensions, Taxes, and Estate Administration in Canada and the Philippines
steps.html:
Once the official death certificates are issued, you can initiate survivor benefit claims, tax filings, and estate settlement in both jurisdictions.

  • Pensions and federal benefits in Canada: Notify Service Canada (1-800-277-9914) to cancel Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) retirement benefits and to apply for the one-time CPP Death Benefit, the CPP Survivor's Pension, and surviving child benefits (or contact Retraite Québec for the Quebec Pension Plan) [8].
  • Tax filings and estate clearance in Canada: Notify the Canada Revenue Agency (1-800-959-8281) to report the date of death, file the Final T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return (and any T3 Trust Return for the estate), and request a Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) before distributing estate assets [9]. Apply for provincial Probate (such as a Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee in Ontario or Grant of Probate in BC) if the deceased held sole-name Canadian assets requiring court authority.
  • Benefits, taxes, and estate settlement in the Philippines: If your family member contributed to Philippine social insurance or held assets in the Philippines, eligible claimants can file for Funeral and Death Benefits with the Social Security System [10] (or GSIS for public-sector employees, plus PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG Fund, and OWWA benefits where applicable). If the deceased left property or bank accounts in the Philippines, heirs or executors must file an Estate Tax Return (BIR Form 1801) with the Bureau of Internal Revenue within one year from the date of death (and complete an Extrajudicial Settlement of Estate before a Philippine notary if there is no will and no contested debts, or judicial probate if there is a will) to obtain the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR) [11].

Have you decided whether to arrange local burial or cremation in the Philippines or to repatriate the body or cremated ashes to Canada?

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in United Kingdom: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in United Kingdom: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in United Kingdom: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in United Kingdom, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and United Kingdom.
introHtml: We are very sorry for the loss of your family member. Managing a death in the United Kingdom for a person with citizenship or residence ties to Canada involves coordinating UK medical, register office, and coroner or Scottish review procedures with Canadian consular, border, and federal or provincial authorities. Below are the five official steps in order.

steps.title: Medical Certification of Death and Coroner or Procurator Fiscal Clearance in the United Kingdom
steps.html:
Before civil registration, funeral arrangements, or international transport can proceed, the cause of death must be certified under the rules of the relevant UK constituent nation [1][2].

  • Expected death in a hospital, hospice, or care setting: In England and Wales, an attending medical practitioner completes the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (MCCD), which is scrutinized and countersigned by an independent NHS Medical Examiner before being transmitted electronically to the local Register Office [1][2]. In Scotland, the doctor issues the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (Form 11), and in Northern Ireland, the attending doctor issues the MCCD reviewed by the Medical Examiner Service [1].
  • Unexpected, sudden, or unexplained death outside a hospital: Call emergency services (999) or NHS 111 immediately so a medical professional and police can verify the death [1]. If the cause of death is unknown, sudden, unnatural, or accidental, the case is referred to the Coroner (in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) or to the Procurator Fiscal within the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (in Scotland), who determines whether a post-mortem examination or inquest is required before releasing the deceased for registration and funeral arrangements [1][2].

steps.title: Insurance Notification, Funeral Coordination, and Consular Assistance
steps.html:
Check immediately whether your family member had travel, medical-assistance, or employer repatriation insurance, as the insurer's assistance team usually appoints the international funeral coordinators directly and covers eligible repatriation costs [3].

  • Consular notification and support: Contact the High Commission of Canada in the United Kingdom at Canada House in London (or the Consulate of Canada in Belfast, or Global Affairs Canada's 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre at +1 613-996-8885 or sos@international.gc.ca) [3][4]. Consular officials can provide guidance on local procedures, assist with locating funeral providers, and cancel the deceased's Canadian passport [3][4].
  • Appointing funeral coordinators: You can mandate a UK funeral director experienced in international repatriation alongside a provincially licensed receiving funeral home in Canada [3][5]. In the UK, families can search professional directories such as the National Association of Funeral Directors (NAFD) or the National Society of Allied and Independent Funeral Directors (+44 1279 726777, info@saif.org.uk) [5]. In Canada, funeral providers are regulated at the provincial level, such as through the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (+1 647-496-4029, info@thebao.ca), Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or member directories of the Funeral Service Association of Canada [6]. These associations and directories are listed as public-source examples for orientation; Clarvia does not endorse, recommend, or rank specific providers.

steps.title: Civil Death Registration in the United Kingdom and Document Legalization for Canada
steps.html:
Once the Medical Certificate of Cause of Death (or coroner's notification) has been sent to the civil registrar, the death must be registered with the local Register Office in the district where the death occurred (for example, Westminster Register Office in London, Manchester Registration Service, or the City of Edinburgh Council Registration Service) [1][2].

  • Statutory registration deadlines: Register the death within 5 days of the registrar receiving the medical certificate in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, or within 8 days in Scotland, and purchase multiple certified copies of the official UK Death Certificate (entry in the register of deaths) [1][2].
  • Apostille and recognition in Canada: Both the United Kingdom and Canada are parties to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention. To ensure UK death certificates are accepted by Canadian banks, courts, and estate institutions without additional consular legalization, apply for a Hague Apostille through the UK Legalisation Office (part of the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office - FCDO) [7]. Note that Canadian provincial Vital Statistics registries (such as ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) only register deaths occurring within their province, so the UK Death Certificate (with FCDO Apostille where required) serves as the official proof of death in Canada [3].

steps.title: International Repatriation to Canada vs. Local Burial or Cremation in the United Kingdom
steps.html:
Your family can choose either to repatriate the body or cremated ashes to Canada or to arrange local burial or cremation in the United Kingdom [1][3].

  • Repatriating human remains (casket) from the UK to Canada: In England and Wales, before a body can be removed outside England or Wales, the local Coroner must be notified on Form 103 and issue an Out-of-England Order (Form 104) after confirming no further inquiries are needed [1]. In Scotland, applications to repatriate human remains outside Scotland require advance clearance from Healthcare Improvement Scotland's Death Certification Review Service (DCRS). Your UK funeral director also arranges arterial embalming, a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin, and a Freedom from Infection Certificate.
  • Canadian border entry requirements (CBSA and Quarantine Act): Upon arrival in Canada, the Canada Border Services Agency enforces Quarantine Act rules (Memorandum D19-9-3), requiring an official Death Certificate stating the cause of death, proof that the person did not die of a Listed Communicable Disease (or hermetically sealed containment), and an embalming/leak-proof casket certificate [8].
  • Transporting cremated ashes to Canada: If cremation takes place in the UK, no Out-of-England Order is required to transport cremated ashes abroad, and the Canada Border Services Agency does not impose Quarantine Act restrictions on cremated remains accompanied by the certified Death Certificate and Certificate of Cremation [3][8].

steps.title: Post-Death Benefits, Pensions, Taxes, and Estate Administration in Canada and the United Kingdom
steps.html:
With the official Death Certificates, you can complete government notifications, survivor benefit claims, tax filings, and probate in both countries.

  • Pensions and federal benefits in Canada: Notify Service Canada (1-800-277-9914) to cancel Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) retirement benefits and to apply for the one-time CPP Death Benefit, the CPP Survivor's Pension, and children's benefits (or contact Retraite Québec for the Quebec Pension Plan) [9].
  • Tax filings and estate clearance in Canada: Notify the Canada Revenue Agency (1-800-959-8281) to report the date of death, file the deceased's Final T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return (and any T3 Trust Return for the estate), and apply for a Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) before distributing assets [10]. Provincial probate (or resealing a UK grant of probate in a Canadian provincial court) is completed in the province where Canadian real estate or financial accounts are held.
  • Notifications, pensions, taxes, and probate in the United Kingdom: When registering the death in England, Scotland, or Wales, ask the registrar for a reference code to use the Tell Us Once service, which notifies HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC), the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP Bereavement Service / International Pension Centre), Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), and local councils in one step [1][11]. If the deceased held UK assets requiring court authority, apply for a Grant of Probate (or Letters of Administration) in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland, or Confirmation through the Sheriff Court in Scotland, via the HM Courts & Tribunals Service Probate portal after reporting the estate value and any Inheritance Tax (Form IHT400) to HMRC [12].

closingQuestion: To tailor these steps to your situation: 1. In which UK nation (England, Scotland, Wales, or Northern Ireland) and city did the death occur, and in which Canadian province or territory was your family member resident? 2. Have you decided whether to arrange local burial or cremation in the United Kingdom or to repatriate the body or cremated ashes to Canada?

title: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in France: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When a Citizen of Canada Dies in France: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement guide when a citizen or resident of Canada dies in France: medical certification and police/coroner clearance in France, licensed funeral providers in both countries, civil death registration and legalization, international repatriation vs. local burial/cremation, and survivor pension & probate steps in Canada and France.
introHtml: Please accept our sincere condolences on the death of your family member. When a person with Canadian citizenship or residence ties to Canada dies in France, the official procedures are coordinated between French medical, municipal, and prefectural authorities and Canadian consular, border, tax, and social security services. Below are the five main official steps in chronological order.

steps.title: Medical Certification of Death and Forensic Clearance in France
steps.html:
Before any civil registration, funeral arrangements, or international transport can take place, the death must be medically certified in France [1][2].

  • Death in a healthcare facility or nursing home (EHPAD): The attending hospital physician issues the medical certificate of death (certificat médical de décès, either on the paper Cerfa form or electronically via the CertDc application), which is required to register the death at the town hall (mairie) and to authorize sealing the coffin [1].
  • Death at home, in a hotel, or in a public place: Immediately call the emergency medical service (SAMU at 15) or the European emergency number (112) so that a physician can attend and certify the death [1].
  • Sudden, accidental, or suspicious death (obstacle médico-légal): If the cause of death is unknown or suspicious, the physician checks the obstacle médico-légal (medico-legal hold) box on the death certificate, and the police or gendarmerie (17) refer the case to the public prosecutor (procureur de la République) [1][2]. The body is then transferred to a forensic medical institute (such as the Institut médico-légal de Paris or the competent university hospital forensic unit), and no funeral operation, cremation, or removal from French territory may take place until the prosecutor's office (parquet) issues formal clearance [1][2].

steps.title: Repatriation Insurance, Licensed Funeral Directors, and Consular Assistance
steps.html:
Before incurring out-of-pocket expenses, check whether your family member had travel insurance, medical assistance coverage (through a credit card, employer, or private policy), or repatriation insurance, as the insurer's assistance center generally appoints and directly pays the funeral providers [3].

  • Canadian consular assistance: Contact the Ambassade du Canada en France (Embassy of Canada to France) in Paris (or the 24/7 Emergency Watch and Response Centre of Global Affairs Canada at +1 613-996-8885 or sos@international.gc.ca) [3][4]. Consular officials can provide a list of local funeral directors experienced in international transfers, guide the family on French procedures, and cancel the deceased person's Canadian passport [3][4].
  • Appointing licensed funeral providers: You may appoint a funeral operator licensed by the French prefecture (opérateur funéraire habilité en préfecture, listed with national bodies such as the Fédération Nationale du Funéraire - FNF or the Fédération Française des Pompes Funèbres - FFPF) in coordination with a licensed receiving funeral home in the destination Canadian province [2][3][5]. In Canada, funeral services are regulated at the provincial level, such as the Bereavement Authority of Ontario (+1 647-496-4029, info@thebao.ca) in Ontario, Consumer Protection BC in British Columbia, or the directory of the Funeral Service Association of Canada [5]. These regulatory bodies and directories are cited as public examples for your orientation; Clarvia does not recommend, endorse, or rank any specific provider.

steps.title: Civil Registration of the Death in France and Document Recognition in Canada
steps.html:
Declaring the death is mandatory and must be completed with the civil status office (service de l'état civil) of the town hall (mairie) where the death occurred (for example, the district town hall in Paris, Lyon, or Marseille, or the local municipal mairie) [1].

  • Statutory timeframe and civil status records in France: The declaration must be made within 24 hours of the medical certification of death (excluding weekends and public holidays), a step most often carried out on the family's behalf by the healthcare facility or appointed funeral operator in accordance with the rules published on Service-Public.fr [1]. Request several full copies of the civil death certificate (copies intégrales de l'acte de décès) as well as multilingual extracts (extraits plurilingues, CIEC Form C under the 1976 Vienna Convention) [1].
  • Apostille and using the French record in Canada: Because both France and Canada are parties to the Hague Apostille Convention of 5 October 1961, a full copy of the French acte de décès intended for Canadian government agencies, banks, or courts can be authenticated with an Apostille issued in France by the Notaires de France through their regional notarial apostille and legalization centers [6][7]. In Canada, provincial civil status registries (such as ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics, or the Directeur de l'état civil in Quebec) generally register only deaths occurring within their provincial boundaries; the French acte de décès (in French, which is an official language at the federal level and in Quebec, or accompanied by a certified English translation for certain English-speaking provincial courts) therefore serves as the official proof of death in Canada [3].

steps.title: International Repatriation to Canada vs. Burial or Cremation in France
steps.html:
The family may choose either international repatriation of the body or cremated ashes to Canada, or local funeral arrangements in France [2][3].

  • Repatriating the body (in a coffin) from France to Canada: The French funeral operator applies to the prefecture of the department where the coffin is sealed for an international mortuary transit permit (laissez-passer mortuaire, issued in accordance with French health regulations and international treaties such as the Berlin Arrangement or Strasbourg Agreement), arranges embalming (soins de conservation / thanatopraxie) if required by the airline, and places the body in a hermetically sealed coffin with a sealed metal liner [2][6]. Upon arrival in Canada, the Agence des services frontaliers du Canada (Canada Border Services Agency, CBSA) enforces the Quarantine Act (Memorandum D19-9-3) and inspects the official death certificate stating the cause of death, the statement confirming the absence of a listed communicable disease (or compliant hermetic sealing), and the embalming or coffin-sealing certificate [8].
  • Transporting cremated ashes to Canada: If cremation takes place in France (authorized by the mayor of the municipality of death or coffin sealing), transporting the cinerary urn to Canada requires the acte de décès and the cremation certificate (certificat de crémation) [2][8]. The Agence des services frontaliers du Canada does not impose quarantine restrictions on cremated human remains accompanied by these certificates [8].

steps.title: Survivor Benefits, Taxation, and Estate Administration in Canada and France
steps.html:
Once the official death certificates have been issued, you can initiate benefit claims, tax filings, and estate administration in both countries.

  • Pensions and survivor benefits in Canada: Notify Service Canada (1-800-277-9915) to stop Old Age Security (OAS) and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) payments and to apply for the CPP Death Benefit, Survivor's Pension, and children's benefits (or contact Retraite Québec if your family member contributed to the Quebec Pension Plan - QPP/RRQ) [9].
  • Tax filings and probate in Canada: Notify the Agence du revenu du Canada (Canada Revenue Agency, CRA, at 1-800-959-7383) of the date of death, file the deceased's Final T1 Income Tax Return (as well as any T3 Trust Return for the estate), and apply for a tax Clearance Certificate (Form TX19) before making the final distribution of estate assets [10]. Depending on the Canadian province of residence or where property is located, the estate executor or liquidator applies for probate (homologation or vérification of the will) with the competent provincial court.
  • Social security benefits, taxation, and notarial succession in France: If the deceased was insured under French social security or held assets in France, eligible beneficiaries may claim the lump-sum death benefit (capital décès) from the local health insurance fund (Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie - CPAM) via Ameli.fr [11], notify L'Assurance Retraite (CNAV) and the supplementary pension scheme Agirc-Arrco to stop retirement pensions and apply for a survivor's pension (pension de réversion) [12], and instruct a French notary's office via the Notaires de France to draw up the deed of heirship (acte de notoriété), settle the French estate, and file the French inheritance tax return (déclaration de succession) with the French tax administration [7].

closingQuestion: To provide guidance tailored to your situation, in which municipality or department in France did the death occur, in which Canadian province or territory did your family member reside, and do you wish to arrange repatriation of the body or ashes to Canada or a local burial or cremation in France?

fr.title: Que faire lors d'un décès entre France et Canada : liste officielle en 5 étapes
fr.cardSummary: Guide officiel en 5 étapes après un décès entre France et Canada : certificat médical de décès, opérateur funéraire habilité, déclaration à l'état civil, démarches consulaires et rapatriement ou inhumation locale, et pensions de réversion et succession.
fr.introHtml: Toutes nos condoléances pour le décès de votre proche. Lorsqu'une personne ayant la citoyenneté canadienne ou des attaches de résidence au Canada décède en France, les démarches s'organisent entre les autorités médicales, municipales et préfectorales françaises et les services consulaires, frontaliers, fiscaux et sociaux canadiens. Voici les cinq grandes étapes officielles dans l'ordre.

steps.title: Constatation médicale du décès et levée d'obstacle médico-légal en France
steps.html:
Avant toute démarche d'état civil, d'obsèques ou de transport international, le décès doit être constaté médicalement en France [1][2].

  • Décès en établissement de santé ou EHPAD : Le médecin du service établit le certificat médical de décès (sur support papier Cerfa ou par voie électronique via l'application CertDc), nécessaire à la déclaration en mairie et à la fermeture du cercueil [1].
  • Décès à domicile, à l'hôtel ou sur la voie publique : Appelez immédiatement le SAMU (15) ou le numéro d'urgence européen (112) afin qu'un médecin constate le décès [1].
  • Décès soudain, accidentel ou suspect (obstacle médico-légal) : Si la cause du décès est inconnue ou suspecte, le médecin coche la case « obstacle médico-légal » sur le certificat de décès et la police ou la gendarmerie (17) saisit le procureur de la République [1][2]. Le corps est alors transféré vers un institut médico-légal (par exemple l'Institut médico-légal de Paris ou du centre hospitalier universitaire compétent) et aucune opération funéraire, crémation ni sortie du territoire ne peut avoir lieu avant la délivrance de l'autorisation du parquet [1][2].

steps.title: Assurance rapatriement, opérateurs funéraires habilités et assistance consulaire
steps.html:
Avant d'engager des frais à titre personnel, vérifiez si votre proche bénéficiait d'une assurance voyage, d'une garantie d'assistance médicale (carte bancaire, employeur ou contrat privé) ou d'une assurance rapatriement, car le plateau d'assistance mandate et règle généralement directement les opérateurs funéraires [3].

  • Assistance consulaire canadienne : Contactez l'Ambassade du Canada en France à Paris (ou le Centre de surveillance et d'intervention d'urgence d'Affaires mondiales Canada ouvert 24h/24 au +1 613-996-8885 ou à sos@international.gc.ca) [3][4]. Les services consulaires peuvent communiquer une liste d'entreprises de pompes funèbres locales expérimentées dans les transferts internationaux, orienter la famille sur les procédures françaises et procéder à l'annulation du passeport canadien de la personne décédée [3][4].
  • Désignation des opérateurs funéraires : Vous pouvez mandater un opérateur funéraire habilité en préfecture en France (répertorié notamment auprès de la Fédération Nationale du Funéraire - FNF ou de la Fédération Française des Pompes Funèbres - FFPF) en coordination avec un salon funéraire récepteur agréé dans la province de destination au Canada [2][3][5]. Au Canada, les services funéraires relèvent de la réglementation provinciale, comme l'organisme Bereavement Authority of Ontario (+1 647-496-4029, info@thebao.ca) en Ontario, Consumer Protection BC en Colombie-Britannique ou le répertoire de l'Association des services funéraires du Canada (Funeral Service Association of Canada) [5]. Ces organismes et répertoires sont mentionnés à titre d'exemples publics pour votre orientation ; Clarvia ne recommande, ne cautionne ni ne classe aucun prestataire.

steps.title: Déclaration du décès à l'état civil en France et reconnaissance documentaire au Canada
steps.html:
La déclaration de décès est obligatoire et doit être effectuée auprès du service de l'état civil de la mairie du lieu de décès (par exemple la mairie d'arrondissement à Paris, Lyon ou Marseille, ou la mairie de la commune concernée) [1].

  • Délai légal et actes d'état civil en France : La déclaration doit intervenir dans les 24 heures suivant la constatation du décès (hors week-ends et jours fériés), démarche que l'établissement de santé ou l'opérateur funéraire mandaté accomplit le plus souvent pour la famille selon les règles publiées sur Service-Public.fr [1]. Demandez plusieurs copies intégrales de l'acte de décès ainsi que des extraits plurilingues (Formule C de la Convention CIEC de Vienne de 1976) [1].
  • Apostille et utilisation de l'acte au Canada : La France et le Canada étant tous deux parties à la Convention de La Haye du 5 octobre 1961, la copie intégrale de l'acte de décès français destinée aux administrations, banques ou tribunaux canadiens peut être revêtue d'une Apostille délivrée en France par les Notaires de France via les centres notariaux d'apostille et de légalisation [6][7]. Au Canada, les registres provinciaux de l'état civil (tels que ServiceOntario, BC Vital Statistics ou le Directeur de l'état civil au Québec) n'enregistrent que les décès survenus sur leur territoire provincial ; l'acte de décès français (en français, langue officielle au niveau fédéral et au Québec, ou accompagné d'une traduction certifiée en anglais pour certaines juridictions provinciales anglophones) constitue donc la preuve officielle du décès au Canada [3].

steps.title: Rapatriement international vers le Canada ou inhumation et crémation en France
steps.html:
La famille peut opter soit pour le rapatriement du corps ou des cendres vers le Canada, soit pour des obsèques locales en France [2][3].

  • Rapatriement du corps (en cercueil) de la France vers le Canada : L'entreprise de pompes funèbres française sollicite auprès de la préfecture du département de fermeture du cercueil un laissez-passer mortuaire international (conformément au cadre sanitaire et aux accords internationaux tels que l'Arrangement de Berlin ou l'Accord de Strasbourg), organise les soins de conservation (thanatopraxie) si requis par la compagnie aérienne, et procède à la mise en bière dans un cercueil hermétique avec enveloppe métallique scellée [2][6]. À l'arrivée au Canada, l'Agence des services frontaliers du Canada applique la Loi sur la mise en quarantaine (Mémorandum D19-9-3) et vérifie le certificat officiel de décès mentionnant la cause du décès, l'attestation d'absence de maladie transmissible inscrite (ou le scellement hermétique conforme) et le certificat de soins de conservation ou d'étanchéité du cercueil [8].
  • Transport des cendres crématoires vers le Canada : Si la crémation a lieu en France (autorisée par le maire de la commune du décès ou de mise en bière), le transport de l'urne cinéraire vers le Canada requiert l'acte de décès et le certificat de crémation [2][8]. L'Agence des services frontaliers du Canada n'applique pas de restrictions de quarantaine aux cendres crématoires accompagnées de ces certificats [8].

steps.title: Prestations de survivant, fiscalité et règlement de la succession au Canada et en France
steps.html:
Une fois les actes de décès obtenus, vous pouvez engager les démarches sociales, fiscales et successorales dans les deux pays.

  • Pensions et prestations au Canada : Informez Service Canada (1-800-277-9915) afin d'interrompre la pension de la Sécurité de la vieillesse (SV) et du Régime de pensions du Canada (RPC) et de demander la prestation de décès du RPC, la pension de survivant et les prestations d'enfants (ou contactez Retraite Québec si votre proche cotisait au Régime de rentes du Québec - RRQ) [9].
  • Impôts et homologation successorale au Canada : Avisez l'Agence du revenu du Canada (1-800-959-7383) de la date du décès, produisez la déclaration finale de revenus T1 (ainsi que toute déclaration de fiducie T3 pour la succession) et demandez le certificat de décharge (formulaire TX19) avant la distribution définitive des biens [10]. Selon la province de résidence ou de situation des biens au Canada, le liquidateur ou fiduciaire de la succession effectue la vérification ou l'homologation du testament (Probate) auprès du tribunal provincial compétent.
  • Prestations sociales, fiscalité et notariat en France : Si la personne décédée était affiliée ou détenait des biens en France, les ayants droit peuvent demander le capital décès auprès de la Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie via Ameli.fr [11], notifier L'Assurance Retraite (CNAV) et l'Agirc-Arrco pour l'arrêt des retraites et la demande de pension de réversion [12], et mandater un office notarial via les Notaires de France pour établir l'acte de notoriété, régler la succession française et déposer la déclaration fiscale de succession auprès de l'administration fiscale française [7].

fr.closingQuestion: Pour vous apporter des précisions adaptées à votre situation : 1. Dans quelle commune ou quel département en France le décès est-il survenu, et dans quelle province ou quel territoire du Canada votre proche résidait-il ? 2. Souhaitez-vous organiser un rapatriement du corps ou des cendres vers le Canada, ou privilégier une inhumation ou une crémation en France ?
